tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.text: Half your users hit a clean 200; the other half get a spinner and a timeout. The room is three commits deep into the request handler — and the real fault is a stale DNS answer resolving to a decommissioned pod. Everyone is debugging the app. Nobody is tracing the path.

The TCP/IP model is not trivia to recite — it is the map you trace when a service is reachable from some clients and dead for others after a DNS, TLS, routing, or policy change. Its job is to tell application symptoms from network causes so you fix the layer that is actually broken.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.prompt: A service works from your laptop but 500s from inside the cluster after a deploy. First instinct: read the new application code? Decide before reading on.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.reveal: The split — works there, fails here — is the tell that the fault lives on the PATH, not in the handler. Same binary, same request, different network vantage: that isolates DNS resolution, route asymmetry, TLS trust, or a NetworkPolicy, not your business logic. Reading the code first debugs the one layer the evidence already cleared. Trace the path, and the 'works for some' pattern points straight at the broken edge.

tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.intro: Running the path trace, one hook at a time. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
tcp-ip-model-without-trivia.code:
## 1. Path Trace — service.example.com fails for ~40% of clients
# L-DNS  does the name resolve to a LIVE endpoint?
dig +short service.example.com          # -> 10.0.4.9 (old pod, terminated)
# L-ROUTE does traffic reach the host at all?
traceroute -n 10.0.4.9                  # -> dies at last hop (no such target)
# L-TLS  is the certificate trusted for THIS name?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify|CN='
# L-HTTP what does the app actually answer once connected?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health   # -> never reaches app: connect timeout
# L-POLICY is a NetworkPolicy silently dropping the pod?
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n orders | grep -A2 'Ingress'

- Suspect layer: DNS — stale A record points at a terminated endpoint
- Blast radius: ~40% of clients (those with the cached answer); no data loss
- Boundary: application handler NOT in scope until the path resolves clean
steps: DNS — the cheapest disqualifier: dig +short is seconds and interrogates the very first layer. A stale A record record explains 'works for some' instantly: clients holding the old cached answer route to a dead IP.
Route — did it even arrive?: traceroute separates 'the packet never reached the host' from 'the host refused it'. A route that dies mid-path is a network cause, never an app bug.
TLS — trusted for THIS name?: openssl s_client with -servername checks SNI + cert validity. A cert valid for the old name but not the new one is the classic silent TLS break after a rename.
HTTP — what the app actually says: curl -v is the first hook that reaches HTTP semantics. If connect times out here, every layer ABOVE the app is still suspect — you have not reached the handler yet.
Policy — the invisible deny: kubectl describe networkpolicy surfaces a rule that drops traffic before the pod ever sees it. A policy deny looks exactly like an app hang from the client side.
The verdict + boundary: Name the suspect layer, the blast radius (stale ≠ lost), and what stays out of scope. The app handler is off-limits until the path is proven clean.

storyboard.say: The symptom: half your users get a clean 200, half get a spinner and a timeout. Same app, same commit.
The room is three commits deep in the app handler. Stop. Don't change code yet — trace the path first.
Layer one, DNS. The client asks 'what IP is this name?' — and this is where working and failing clients diverge.
Here's the fault: DNS resolves to a stale IP — a decommissioned pod. Half the users route straight to a dead endpoint.
Prove it downstream: a good IP reaches the host, TLS completes a trusted handshake, the gateway forwards.
NetworkPolicy allows the forward and the Service answers — the whole spine is healthy once the IP is correct.
Only now does the app handler run. It was never the cause — it just inherited a spinner from a bad name lookup.
The lesson: name the layer where working and failing clients disagree, before you touch a single line of code.

options: Re-read the application handler, since it changed in the deploy.
Run dig +short against the name from a failing client and check whether it resolves to a live endpoint — a check whose answer eliminates or confirms the DNS layer.
Redeploy the service and see if the problem goes away.
Add more logging to the endpoint so you have something to show.

Re-reading code (1) debugs the layer the evidence cleared; redeploy (3) and more logging (4) buy no information about which layer is broken.

packet-path-reasoning.text: It works from your laptop and fails for half of production. The channel fills with app-code theories while the real fault is a stale DNS answer, an untrusted cert, an asymmetric route, or a NetworkPolicy that silently drops the packet — three hops before your code ever runs.

In Network Mental Models you learned the layers exist; packet path reasoning is the move that makes them pay off. It converts 'the service is flaky' into one directed path with a single failing hop you can point a command at — the trace that anchors every incident in this course.

packet-path-reasoning.prompt: A service is reachable from some clients and dead for others after a routine deploy. Your first instinct is to read the service's own logs. Good instinct — or a trap? Answer before reading on.
packet-path-reasoning.reveal: A trap. 'Reachable for some, dead for others' is the fingerprint of a NETWORK cause — DNS returning different answers per resolver, a cert some clients won't trust, route asymmetry, or a policy that only allows some source ranges. The service's own logs show it happily serving whoever reaches it, which quietly convinces you the code is fine and burns an hour. The packet often dies before it arrives — so trace the path first, read app logs last.

packet-path-reasoning.intro: Tracing the path with four inspection hooks. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
packet-path-reasoning.code:
# Hop 1 — DNS: does the name resolve, and to the SAME IP everywhere?
dig +short service.example.com            # us: 10.0.42.7   |  failing region: NXDOMAIN

# Hop 2/3 — route + TLS: can we connect, and is the cert chain trusted?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
#   * Connected to service.example.com (10.0.42.7) port 443   <- route OK
#   * SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer cert  <- TLS FAILS here

# Confirm the TLS verdict directly (independent of curl's trust store)
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify|subject='
#   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)   <- missing intermediate

# Hop 5 — policy: rule out a silent drop as an alternative cause
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-frontend -n web | grep -A3 Ingress
#   From: podSelector app=frontend  (source range is allowed — not the cause here)
steps: Hop 1 — DNS first, always: dig +short from a passing AND a failing vantage. Different answers (or NXDOMAIN for one region) means the packet never even aims at the right IP — stop here.

Hops 2–3 — route then TLS in one shot: curl -v prints 'Connected to <IP>' (route survived) then the TLS verdict. 'unable to get local issuer certificate' is a trust failure, not an app failure — the request dies mid-handshake.

Confirm TLS independently: openssl s_client bypasses curl's trust store. 'Verify return code: 21' pins it: the server isn't sending its intermediate cert, so clients without it cached reject the chain — exactly the 'some pass, some fail' split.

Hop 5 — rule policy IN or OUT: A NetworkPolicy that drops your source range produces the identical 'some clients fail' symptom. Checking it turns 'probably TLS' into 'TLS, and NOT a silent policy drop.'
packet-path-reasoning.commonMistake: False confidence — nothing a reviewer can replay

packet-path-reasoning.title: Trace the path before you change the system
packet-path-reasoning.text: Walk one request hop by hop — DNS lookup, IP route, TLS trust, HTTP/proxy semantics, firewall + NetworkPolicy — and find the first hop that fails. Separate what you can directly observe from what you infer. The failing hop, not the loudest service, is the cause.

packet-path-reasoning.title: The packet path — and where it dies
packet-path-reasoning.subtitle: One request, five decision points. The suspect hop (TLS trust) fails a subset of clients; the app never sees the request. DNS, route, and policy are the other places the packet can die before your code runs.

legend.label: app: sees only requests that survived the path

storyboard.say: One request starts at the client. It works from your laptop but fails for half of production, and the channel fills with app-code theories.
Hop one: the client resolves the name. A stale DNS answer can point half your clients at the wrong IP before anything connects.
Hop two: DNS hands back an IP and the client routes to it. An asymmetric route or bad NAT can silently swallow the packet here.
Hop three, the suspect: the TLS handshake. An untrusted cert fails a subset of clients, and the app never even sees the request.
Hop four: only after trust is established does the HTTP request reach the load balancer or proxy — real bytes, real semantics.
Hop five: the proxy asks to admit the request, and a NetworkPolicy can silently drop it right before delivery.
Only if every hop passes is the request delivered to your service. The failing hop, not the loudest service, is the cause.

packet-path-reasoning.title: Tracing the path with four inspection hooks
packet-path-reasoning.subtitle: The exact commands from the decision packet — each one kills or confirms one hop. Run them in path order, top to bottom.
packet-path-reasoning.code:
# Hop 1 — DNS: does the name resolve, and to the SAME IP everywhere?
dig +short service.example.com            # us: 10.0.42.7   |  failing region: NXDOMAIN

# Hop 2/3 — route + TLS: can we connect, and is the cert chain trusted?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
#   * Connected to service.example.com (10.0.42.7) port 443   <- route OK
#   * SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer cert  <- TLS FAILS here

# Confirm the TLS verdict directly (independent of curl's trust store)
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify|subject='
#   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)   <- missing intermediate

# Hop 5 — policy: rule out a silent drop as an alternative cause
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-frontend -n web | grep -A3 Ingress
#   From: podSelector app=frontend  (source range is allowed — not the cause here)

steps.label: Hop 1 — DNS first, always
steps.note: dig +short from a passing AND a failing vantage. Different answers (or NXDOMAIN for one region) means the packet never even aims at the right IP — stop here.

steps.label: Hops 2–3 — route then TLS in one shot
steps.note: curl -v prints 'Connected to <IP>' (route survived) then the TLS verdict. 'unable to get local issuer certificate' is a trust failure, not an app failure — the request dies mid-handshake.

steps.label: Confirm TLS independently
steps.note: openssl s_client bypasses curl's trust store. 'Verify return code: 21' pins it: the server isn't sending its intermediate cert, so clients without it cached reject the chain — exactly the 'some pass, some fail' split.

steps.label: Hop 5 — rule policy IN or OUT
steps.note: A NetworkPolicy that drops your source range produces the identical 'some clients fail' symptom. Checking it turns 'probably TLS' into 'TLS, and NOT a silent policy drop.'

packet-path-reasoning.caption: Two hooks confirm the cause (curl + openssl → cert chain), one rules out the look-alike (policy). That's decision proof + operational proof in four commands.

packet-path-reasoning.text: The senior tell in networking: 'reachable for some, broken for others' is almost never the application. It is per-resolver DNS, a cert chain missing its intermediate, route/NAT asymmetry, or a NetworkPolicy scoped to a subset of sources. A staff engineer distrusts symmetric app theories the moment the failure is asymmetric across clients — because the packet path, not the code, is where clients diverge.

packet-path-reasoning.question: A reviewer challenges your incident packet: 'You say it's a TLS trust issue — prove it's the network and not our code.' Which evidence actually settles it?
options: The service's own logs show no errors, so the code must be fine.

openssl s_client returns 'Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)' from a failing client and a clean handshake from a passing one — the request dies in the handshake, before any HTTP reaches the app.
You redeployed the service and it felt more stable afterward.
A teammate agrees it's 'probably a cert thing.'
packet-path-reasoning.explanation: Only option 2 is executable and layer-specific: the handshake fails on failing clients and succeeds on passing ones, so the packet dies at the TLS hop before HTTP — the app literally never receives the request. Quiet app logs (1) are consistent with a request that never arrived; a redeploy (3) and a teammate's vibe (4) prove nothing and can't be replayed by the reviewer.

latency-and-throughput.doNotClaim: Do not claim the service is 'slow' and stop there. 'Slow' is not a diagnosis — it hides whether each request is slow (latency) or too few fit through the pipe (throughput). Naming 'add more replicas' before you know which axis is bounded is a fix wearing a diagnosis's clothes.

latency-and-throughput.text: The dashboard is green on CPU, green on error rate, and the VP wants '/health made fast by Friday.' Three engineers are already sizing up a bigger load balancer — nobody has yet asked whether one request is slow or whether too many requests are queued behind each other. Those are two different bugs with two opposite fixes.

Latency is how long ONE request takes end to end; throughput is how many requests the path completes per second. They trade off and they fail differently — and confusing them is the classic networking miss where the team scales the wrong thing while the real bound sits in DNS, a TLS handshake, or a saturated link. This is the mental model the rest of the module debugs on top of.

latency-and-throughput.prompt: curl reports 40ms for a single /health call, yet under load p99 climbs to 4s. Is the service 'slow'? Which axis is actually bounded — and why does the single-shot 40ms almost prove the answer? Decide before reading.
latency-and-throughput.reveal: It is a throughput bound, not a latency bound. A lone request is fast (40ms), so the per-hop delay is fine — the 4s under load is queuing: requests arriving faster than the path drains, waiting in line. That is Little's Law in the wild (L = λ × W): raise arrival rate λ against a fixed service capacity and the queue length L — and therefore wait W — explodes, even though each request's own work never changed. 'Add a CDN to cut latency' would do nothing; you needed more concurrency or a faster service, not a shorter path.

latency-and-throughput.intro: The kill-test that separates the two axes. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
latency-and-throughput.code:
# 1. LATENCY: one request, cold path, timing broken out per phase
curl -w 'dns:%{time_namelookup} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n' \
  -o /dev/null -s https://service.example.com/health
# -> dns:0.031 tls:0.088 ttfb:0.040 total:0.129   (one request is FAST)

# 2. THROUGHPUT: saturate the path, watch p99 and req/s
hey -z 30s -c 200 https://service.example.com/health
# -> Requests/sec: 512   p99 latency: 3.98s   (throughput floor + queuing blowup)

# 3. DISQUALIFY the latency story: is any single hop slow?
dig service.example.com +stats            # resolver RTT sane? (rules out DNS latency)
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null
# handshake completes in one round -> TLS is not the per-request cost

# VERDICT: single=129ms, saturated p99=3.98s at 512 req/s
# -> bounded on THROUGHPUT (queuing), NOT per-request latency
steps: Measure one request's latency, per phase: curl -w breaks total into DNS, TLS (appconnect), and TTFB. If total is small, no single hop is the per-request villain — latency is fine.

Saturate to expose the throughput ceiling: hey -c 200 drives concurrency. Requests/sec is the real throughput; the p99 blow-up is queuing, not slower work — each request still does 129ms of actual work.

Rule out latency hops explicitly: dig confirms resolver RTT is sane; openssl confirms the handshake is one round-trip, not a renegotiation. Both are the 'kill-tests' that eliminate the latency branch.

Write the verdict as a gap: 129ms single vs 3.98s saturated is a ~30x gap from concurrency alone. That gap is the signature of a throughput bound. Record the two numbers — they are the evidence a reviewer replays.

latency-and-throughput.title: The request path — where latency accrues and where throughput is capped
latency-and-throughput.subtitle: One request pays latency at every hop (DNS → TLS → gateway → service → DB). Throughput is capped at the narrowest stage: here the connection pool. The queue in front of it is where a throughput bound masquerades as latency.

legend.label: throughput cap — queue forms here under load
service time (the axis a bigger box actually helps)

storyboard.say: One request starts at the client and pays for latency at every hop it takes across the path — nothing here is free.
First the client resolves the name in DNS, then completes a TLS handshake — two round trips that add up before any real work begins.
The connected request reaches the API gateway, the front door where all traffic converges and the path narrows.
Here the request waits: the gateway hands it to a connection-pool queue and it must await a free slot before proceeding.
The queue dequeues only as fast as the pool allows — throughput is capped at pool size, the single narrowest stage on the path.
The worker finally queries Postgres and returns. One request measures latency; a saturated path measures throughput.
Under load, the queue turns a throughput bound into apparent latency — so a bigger load balancer wouldn't touch this pool ceiling.

latency-and-throughput.text: The senior tell is knowing tail latency and throughput are governed together by queuing theory: as you push utilization toward 100% of a resource's throughput, wait time doesn't rise linearly — it goes vertical (the M/M/1 knee). That is why a service humming at 'only 85% CPU' can have a screaming p99. The number that predicts your 2 a.m. page is headroom-to-saturation, not average latency.

latency-and-throughput.question: A single curl to /orders returns in 90ms, but at 300 concurrent users p99 is 6s and DNS/TLS both measure clean. Which is the bounded axis and the correct class of fix?
options: Latency — put the service behind a CDN and use a closer region to cut round-trip time.
Throughput — the fast single request plus clean DNS/TLS point to queuing at a capacity ceiling; raise concurrency/pool size or reduce per-request service time.
Latency — the 6s p99 is the true per-request cost, so optimize the code path on the hot request.
Neither — 6s p99 under load is normal and needs no action.
latency-and-throughput.explanation: The lone request is fast (90ms) and DNS/TLS are clean, so no per-request hop is the villain — the 6s only appears under concurrency, which is the signature of queuing behind a throughput cap. The fix class is capacity/concurrency (more slots or less service time per request), not a CDN or region move (option 1), which target latency the diagnosis just ruled out.

failure-domain-mapping.text: It works from your laptop, it works from staging, and it is down for 30% of production — the same binary, the same request, a different answer depending on WHERE the client sits. The room is already three commits deep into the application code, and the real fault is one CIDR the new NetworkPolicy forgot to allow.

A request is not one hop — it is a chain: DNS resolve, IP route, TLS trust, HTTP semantics, load balancer, firewall, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy. Failure-domain mapping is the move that asks 'which link is actually broken?' before anyone touches code — the release/review-risk section of the incident packet you carry through this module.

failure-domain-mapping.prompt: A service is up for some clients and returns errors for others after a deploy. Your instinct says 'check the application logs first.' Is that the fastest path to the cause? Decide before reading on.
failure-domain-mapping.reveal: Usually no — it is searching where the light is good. 'Works for some clients, not others' is the signature of a DOMAIN split, not a code bug: split-horizon DNS returning different IPs, a certificate whose SAN is trusted by one client store and not another, an asymmetric route where the reply path is dropped, or a NetworkPolicy that allows one CIDR and denies another. The same request hitting the same code gets two answers only when something BELOW the code differs by client. Read the app logs and you will find a symptom; trace the path and you will find the cause.

failure-domain-mapping.intro: The inspection hooks that pin the domain. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
failure-domain-mapping.code:
# 1. DNS — does every client resolve the SAME address?
dig +short service.example.com          # A: 10.0.4.12   B: 10.0.4.12  -> DNS cleared

# 2. TLS — is the served cert trusted and does the SAN match?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'subject=|Verify return code'
#   subject=CN=service.example.com   Verify return code: 0 (ok)  -> TLS cleared

# 3. HTTP — verbose, to see WHERE it stalls (connect? handshake? response?)
curl -v --max-time 5 https://service.example.com/health
#   * Connected to 10.0.4.12 ... then hangs, no response  -> stalls AFTER connect, BELOW HTTP

# 4. Kubernetes NetworkPolicy — the suspect: does an ingress rule cover client B's CIDR?
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-clients -n orders
#   Allowing ingress from: 10.0.4.0/24   (client B is 10.0.9.0/24)  -> CONVICTED: policy drops B
steps: Clear DNS first (cheapest disqualifier): If A and B resolve to different IPs, the domain is split-horizon DNS and you stop here. Same IP for both → DNS is cleared, move down. Observed, not inferred.
Clear TLS trust: 'Verify return code: 0' with a matching SAN clears certificate trust. A code 21/verify failure that differs by client store is your domain — do not go deeper.

curl -v localizes the stall: Verbose curl shows the exact phase. 'Connected ... then hangs' means the TCP path is fine but nothing comes back — the drop is above connect and below HTTP: a policy or firewall silently discarding packets.

Convict the NetworkPolicy: The ingress rule allows 10.0.4.0/24; client B lives in 10.0.9.0/24. That single CIDR gap is the failure domain — packets from B are dropped before the Pod. This line IS the proof.
Repair + re-run: Add 10.0.9.0/24 to the ingress rule, then re-run curl -v from B. A response on the same hook is the before/after evidence the reviewer replays.

storyboard.say: Same binary, same request — but it's down for 30% of production. The client sends the request and it enters the chain at DNS resolve.
First we clear DNS: both clients resolve the same IP, so the domain isn't guessed — it's pinned to the same route.
The route reaches the edge and TLS trust completes — the handshake succeeds, so transport is cleared too.
Now the request hits the NetworkPolicy. For client B the packet is dropped — a silent DENY, not an application error.
Because DNS, route, and TLS were cleared first, the failure domain is named: the firewall layer is where clients diverge.
The repair adds B's CIDR to the allowlist and re-runs the hooks, so B's traffic is now permitted.
The insight: an application symptom is not a network cause. Trace the chain, prove which link breaks, then fix that one CIDR.

dns-resolution.text: The service is up. Half the fleet reaches service.example.com fine; the other half gets connection refused after last night's cutover. Three engineers are already deep in the application logs — and the real fork happened three hops earlier, when two client resolvers returned two different A records for the same name.

This lesson opens the DNS / HTTP / TLS / QUIC module because name resolution is the first hop of every request — the answer chosen here decides which IP, which route, and which certificate everything downstream trusts. The recurring failure it kills: the team debugs application code while the real cause is that different clients are resolving the name to different answers.

dns-resolution.prompt: A service is reachable from some clients and refused by others. curl fails on the broken clients. Where do you look FIRST — the application, the load balancer, or somewhere earlier? Answer before reading on.
dns-resolution.reveal: Earlier. Before a single byte of HTTP is sent, the client must turn the name into an IP — and 'reachable for some, not others' is the signature of a resolution split: stale cache, a resolver pointing at a different view (split-horizon), a TTL that hasn't expired on half the fleet, or an NXDOMAIN on a stub resolver. Run `dig service.example.com` from a WORKING client and a BROKEN client. If the A records differ, you have found the fork before you have opened a single line of application code.

dns-resolution.intro: Tracing the fork with the inspection hooks. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
dns-resolution.code:
# 1. What answer does the FAILING client actually get?
dig +noall +answer service.example.com
# service.example.com. 42 IN A 10.2.4.9      <- stale: old IP, TTL still counting down

# 2. What is the TRUTH, straight from the authoritative NS (bypass every cache)?
dig +norecurse @ns1.example.com service.example.com
# service.example.com. 300 IN A 10.2.9.30    <- cutover IP the working clients have

# 3. Confirm the symptom is downstream of the wrong IP, not the app
curl -v --resolve service.example.com:443:10.2.9.30 https://service.example.com/health
# * Connected to service.example.com (10.2.9.30) port 443 -> 200 OK

# 4. Rule out a TLS-trust red herring on the correct IP
openssl s_client -connect 10.2.9.30:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates
steps: Read the failing client's answer: dig against the resolver the broken client uses. The stale A record (10.2.4.9) with a live TTL is the fork — half the fleet still cached the pre-cutover IP.

Get ground truth from authoritative: +norecurse @ns1 bypasses every cache and asks the zone's source of truth directly. 10.2.9.30 is the correct post-cutover answer. Two different answers for one name = a resolution split, confirmed.
Prove the app is innocent: curl --resolve pins the correct IP, skipping DNS entirely. A 200 here proves the application and route are healthy — the ONLY variable was the resolved IP.
Clear TLS as a confound: openssl s_client checks the cert on the correct IP matches the SNI name and is in date — so you can rule out cert trust before writing 'DNS' in the packet.

storyboard.say: Every request starts here: the app calls getaddrinfo(), asking the local stub resolver to turn a name into an IP.
The stub can't answer itself, so it hands a recursive query to the recursive resolver — the hop that does the real work.
On a cache miss, the recursive resolver walks outward: it asks the root and TLD servers, which refer it down to the authoritative nameserver.
The authoritative nameserver is the source of truth — it returns the real A record straight back to the recursive resolver.
Here's the fork: the recursive resolver caches that answer under a TTL — but on the failing client it's holding a STALE record from before the cutover.
The cached answer flows back to the app, which trusts it blindly to pick the IP, open TLS, and route the request.
So half the fleet gets the new IP and half gets the stale one. Prove which A record the FAILING client resolved before you touch application code.

dns-resolution.text: Read the TTL, not just the A record. RFC 1035 makes TTL the contract: a record cached with TTL 3600 can serve a stale answer for up to an hour after you 'fixed' DNS. The senior move before any cutover is to lower the TTL first, wait one old-TTL interval, THEN change the record — so the fleet converges in minutes instead of an unpredictable hour of split-brain resolution.

dns-resolution.question: A reviewer challenges: 'Show me the exact evidence that this is name resolution and not the application.' Which single piece of evidence best proves it?
options: A screenshot of the application error page from a failing client.
`dig` output from the failing client showing a stale A record, alongside an authoritative `dig @ns1` showing the correct IP — plus `curl --resolve` returning 200 when pinned to the correct IP.
The application logs showing connection-refused errors.
A statement that caches were flushed and the problem improved.
dns-resolution.explanation: Option 2 is the only inspectable chain: it shows the failing client resolved the wrong IP (dig), establishes ground truth from authoritative (dig @ns1), and proves the app is healthy on the correct IP (curl --resolve), isolating the resolved IP as the single variable. The error page (1) and logs (3) are symptoms consistent with many causes; 'flushed and it improved' (4) is correlation with no record of the actual answers, so it cannot be replayed or falsified.

http-semantics.text: The checkout endpoint returns 200 for the office VPN and hangs for half of mobile users after last night's ingress change. Three engineers are reading the order handler line by line — while the real fault is a POST being silently retried through an asymmetric route, double-charging the ones who reconnect.

HTTP semantics is the contract that says what a method promises (safe? idempotent?), what a status class means, and what is safe to retry — and that contract is what breaks first when DNS, TLS, or routing shifts underneath a service. This is Section 3 of the same incident packet you carry through this module, sitting between TLS trust and the proxy/load-balancer behavior above it.

http-semantics.prompt: A client sends POST /orders, the connection drops before any response arrives, and the client library retries. Is that safe? Answer before reading on.
http-semantics.reveal: Only if the server made POST idempotent — and by default it did not. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS are SAFE and idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST is neither. A dropped connection is ambiguous: the request may have committed on the server even though no response reached the client. Retrying a non-idempotent POST across a flaky or asymmetric route is how one checkout becomes two charges. The fix is an Idempotency-Key, not more logging in the handler.

http-semantics.subtitle: A POST /orders traverses DNS → TLS → gateway → two backends behind a policy. The retry (dashed) is only safe if the method is idempotent; the return path is asymmetric, so the client sees a timeout while the write commits. Payments settlement is out of scope.

storyboard.say: A checkout POST starts at the client, which first resolves the hostname through DNS before any bytes move.
DNS hands off to the TLS layer, where the client opens a secure connection to terminate the handshake.
Over that trusted channel, the POST /orders request reaches the API gateway, the front door for this write.
The gateway forwards to the Orders service, which commits to Postgres — a real, non-idempotent side effect.
The response flows back toward the client but hits the NetworkPolicy, which silently drops the return path.
The route is asymmetric: the write succeeded, but the client never sees the reply and reads it as a timeout.
So the client auto-retries the POST — but replaying a non-idempotent request over an unproven path double-charges the user.
The lesson: HTTP idempotency is the contract, and only idempotent methods are safe to retry when the path shifts underneath.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.reveal: The server is not sending its full certificate chain. Your browser silently patched the gap from a cached intermediate it fetched earlier (AIA fetching); curl and many API clients do not. The leaf is valid, the root is trusted — the missing link is the intermediate CA in between. 'It works in my browser' is the false-positive that hides an incomplete chain from every non-browser client on the network.

# Probe the exact chain the server sends for this SNI hostname
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 \
  -servername service.example.com -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl_chain_dump

#   Certificate chain

#   verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
#   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)

# Compare against the client's real trust store, non-browser:
curl -v https://service.example.com/health 2>&1 | grep -Ei 'SSL|subject|issuer|verify'

# Confirm SNI routing: does a different name get a different cert?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 \
  -servername OTHER-vhost.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep 'subject='

storyboard.say: The client opens the connection with a ClientHello — this is the very first message of the TLS handshake.
Inside that hello is the SNI: the hostname the client actually wants, so the server knows which certificate to serve.
The server matches the SNI name and selects a certificate, packing it into the Cert message it sends back.
That message must present both the leaf cert and the intermediate CA — the leaf alone is not enough.
The client walks the chain: the leaf is signed by the intermediate, and the intermediate chains up to a trusted root.
Here is the fault: if the server omits the intermediate, clients that already cache it succeed while everyone else fails.
The padlock lies because trust is per-client — the fix is serving the full chain, not rewriting the app error handler.

tls-handshake-and-certificates.text: The senior tell in TLS incidents: never trust a browser as your test client. Browsers hide server misconfiguration with AIA intermediate-fetching, cached OCSP, and per-vendor root stores. Your API callers, mobile SDKs, and Kubernetes sidecars use a strict CA bundle and no fetching — so 'works in my browser, fails in curl' is not a fluke, it is the exact signature of an incomplete chain or a client-trust-store gap.

quic-tradeoffs.text: You flip the service to HTTP/3 on Friday. Latency drops for most users — and then a corporate customer whose firewall silently drops UDP/443 can't reach you at all, while your dashboards stay green because they only measure the clients that connected.

QUIC rides UDP and folds TLS 1.3 into the handshake, so it buys you 0-RTT resumption and connection migration — but it also moves you off the TCP path every middlebox on Earth already trusts. This lesson lives in Module 2 because you've traced DNS, HTTP, and TLS separately; QUIC is where those layers collapse into one flight and the tradeoff becomes a release decision.

quic-tradeoffs.prompt: Your load test says QUIC cuts p50 connection time by 40%. Is that enough to ship HTTP/3 to all clients? Answer before reading on.
quic-tradeoffs.reveal: No — the load test only measured clients that completed a QUIC handshake. The population that matters most is the one your test can't see: users behind firewalls, NATs, or middleboxes that block or mangle UDP/443. QUIC's real design bet is the fallback: a browser races QUIC against TCP+TLS and quietly drops to HTTP/2 when UDP fails. Your 40% win is real for the reachable; the decision is about the unreachable, and 'faster' says nothing about them.

# Network Path Debug & Incident Packet — HTTP/3 (QUIC) rollout
## Context
Move api.example.com from HTTP/2 (TCP/443) to HTTP/3 (QUIC, UDP/443).
Constraint: 12% of traffic is enterprise clients behind egress firewalls.
## Selected approach
Dual-stack: advertise h3 via Alt-Svc, KEEP TCP+TLS/HTTP2 listening.
## Rejected approach
UDP-only HTTP/3 (drop TCP). Rejected: any UDP-blocking middlebox = hard outage.
## Verify (inspection hooks)
dig +short api.example.com                 # A/AAAA resolve first — rule out DNS
curl -sI --http3-only https://api.example.com/health   # QUIC-only: expect FAIL from corp
curl -sI --http2      https://api.example.com/health   # fallback path: expect 200
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -tls1_3 -alpn h2  </dev/null | grep -E 'ALPN|Verify'
## Expected failure (the QUIC-specific one)
UDP/443 dropped silently by firewall -> handshake never completes ->
dashboards stay green (only measure connected clients) -> corp users dark.
## Reviewer objection
"Is HTTP/3 proven reachable, or only fast for clients that got through?"
## Repair notes
Keep Alt-Svc TTL short; alert on h3:h2 negotiation ratio drop, not just p50.
steps: Constraint before fix: Name WHO is on the path (12% enterprise, egress firewalls) before naming HTTP/3. The constraint is what rules the rejected option out.

The rejected option, with a reason: UDP-only is the seductive answer — fewer sockets, pure QUIC. Rejected because one UDP-blocking middlebox turns a speed win into a hard outage for the client who complains loudest.
Hook 1 — rule out DNS first: dig confirms name resolution isn't the cause. Networking's #1 trap: debugging the app while the real issue is resolution, trust, or policy.
Hooks 2+3 — force each path: --http3-only proves the QUIC path FAILS from a blocked client (the failure trigger); --http2 proves the fallback SUCCEEDS. Two commands, one falsifiable decision.
Hook 4 — confirm ALPN + trust on fallback: openssl shows the TCP path negotiates h2 with a valid cert chain — the fallback isn't just reachable, it's TLS-sound.
The invalidation condition: Green dashboards that only measure connected clients are the false-confidence trap. The repair alerts on the h3:h2 ratio — a reachability signal, not a latency one.

quic-tradeoffs.text: QUIC = TLS 1.3 + streams over UDP/443: 1-RTT (0-RTT on resume), no head-of-line blocking, survives IP changes via connection ID. The cost: UDP is second-class on the internet, so reachability now depends on fallback to TCP+TLS.

quic-tradeoffs.title: Two clients, one origin — where QUIC wins and where it must fall back
quic-tradeoffs.subtitle: The happy path (UDP/443 open) gets 0-RTT and migration. The blocked path (firewall drops UDP) MUST fail over to TCP+TLS/HTTP2 or the customer sees an outage. The fallback edge is the whole decision.

legend.label: the fallback that saves the customer

storyboard.say: You flip to HTTP/3. The mobile client sends QUIC over UDP/443 and gets a 0-RTT handshake straight to the load balancer.
QUIC's payoff: when the phone changes IP, the connection ID lets it migrate to the origin without a new handshake.
Now the corporate client tries the same QUIC attempt, but its packets first hit the company firewall.
Here's the trap: the firewall silently drops UDP. No error, no reset — the client just hears nothing back.
This is the whole decision point. A race timer expires and the corp client must fall back to TCP with TLS 1.3 and HTTP/2.
TCP on 443 is the path every middlebox trusts, so it reaches the load balancer and the customer stays online.
The origin serves h2 or h3 to whoever arrives — the insight: QUIC's speed is real, but reachability lives in the fallback.

quic-tradeoffs.text: The standards make the fallback advisory, not mandatory: HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) over QUIC is typically discovered via the Alt-Svc header (RFC 7838) advertised over an existing HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 origin — so the client usually only tries QUIC after it already has a TCP-based answer, but per RFC 7838 using the alternative is OPTIONAL. That's why 'HTTP/3-only' fights the protocol's own design. The senior tell: you don't measure a QUIC rollout by p50, you measure it by the h3-vs-h2 negotiation ratio — the clients quietly on h2 are your reachability canary.

quic-tradeoffs.question: A reviewer asks: 'Prove your HTTP/3 rollout is reachable, not just fast.' Which evidence answers the challenge?
options: A load test showing QUIC cuts p50 connection time 40% for clients that connected.
curl --http3-only failing from a UDP-blocked client AND curl --http2 returning 200 for that same client, plus an alert on the h3:h2 negotiation ratio.
A statement that browsers 'handle fallback automatically,' so no test is needed.
openssl output proving the TLS 1.3 certificate chain is valid on UDP/443.
quic-tradeoffs.explanation: Reachability is proven by exercising the FAILURE path and the fallback: --http3-only must be able to fail (option 1 only measures the reachable, so it's blind to the population at risk), and --http2 must succeed for that same blocked client. cidr-and-subnets.text: Two teams peer their VPCs on launch day and everything east-west goes dark — both quietly chose 10.0.0.0/16, so the router has two identical destinations and silently drops half the traffic. Nobody touched application code; the whole outage was an address-space decision made months earlier with no overlap check.

CIDR is how you carve a finite address space into non-overlapping, right-sized boundaries — the substrate every route, firewall rule, and peering connection is written against. Get the split wrong and the failure shows up later as asymmetric routing or a silent policy drop that looks like an app bug. This is Section 1 of a decision packet you carry through the routing and load-balancing module.

cidr-and-subnets.prompt: You need room for 500 hosts in a subnet. Someone reaches for a /24. Before you agree — what breaks, and what should the prefix be? Answer before reading on.
cidr-and-subnets.reveal: A /24 gives 256 addresses and only 254 usable — it cannot hold 500 hosts. Each subnet loses TWO addresses: the network address (all-zero host bits) and the broadcast address (all-one host bits). For 500 hosts you need a /23 (512 total, 510 usable). The trap is thinking a /24 means '256 usable' and that bigger numbers after the slash mean bigger networks — it is the reverse: a SMALLER prefix means MORE hosts. /23 is bigger than /24.

cidr-and-subnets.intro: Proving the split with ipcalc, one line at a time. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
cidr-and-subnets.code:
# CIDR Plan — VPC 10.20.0.0/16  (65,536 addresses total)
$ ipcalc 10.20.0.0/16
Network:   10.20.0.0/16
HostMin:   10.20.0.1    HostMax: 10.20.255.254   Hosts: 65534

# Public tier  — LBs + NAT gateways (one /20 spans both AZs)
#   10.20.0.0/20   -> HostMin 10.20.0.1   HostMax 10.20.15.254   (4094 usable)
# App tier AZ-a  10.20.16.0/20 -> 10.20.16.1  .. 10.20.31.254  (4094 usable)
# App tier AZ-b  10.20.32.0/20 -> 10.20.32.1  .. 10.20.47.254  (4094 usable)
# Data tier      10.20.48.0/22 -> 10.20.48.1  .. 10.20.51.254  (1022 usable)

# Overlap check vs peered on-prem 10.10.0.0/16 -> DISJOINT (10.20 != 10.10). PASS
# Rejected: single flat /24 per tier -> 254 hosts, too small for app fleet. REJECT
steps: Anchor the parent: A /16 = 2^16 = 65,536 addresses, 65,534 usable. This is the budget every child spends from — you cannot allocate more than this.
Public /20 carved from the top: A /20 = 2^(32-20) = 4096 addresses, 4094 usable. HostMin is network+1, HostMax is broadcast−1. Spans both AZs on purpose — LBs are AZ-agnostic here.
Two app /20s, one per AZ: AZ-a starts at .16.0 and AZ-b at .32.0 — the next /20 boundary each time. Aligning on the boundary is what guarantees no overlap; an off-boundary start collides.
Data tier sized tight: A /22 = 1022 usable — plenty for a managed DB subnet group, and small on purpose so the blast radius of a data-tier rule is contained.

The overlap check (the whole point): Second octet 20 vs 10 differ, so the two /16s are disjoint — no route ambiguity across the peering link. This is the line that would have prevented the launch-day outage.
The rejected option, on the record: A flat /24 per tier caps at 254 hosts. Naming why it fails under the growth constraint is what turns a pick into a decision.

cidr-and-subnets.title: A prefix draws the line between network and host bits
cidr-and-subnets.text: CIDR /n fixes the first n bits as the network; the remaining 32−n are host bits. Usable hosts = 2^(32−n) − 2 (network + broadcast reserved). Smaller n means a bigger block. The invariant: subnets under one parent must not overlap.

cidr-and-subnets.title: Splitting 10.20.0.0/16 into a non-overlapping VPC plan
cidr-and-subnets.subtitle: One /16 parent carved into public, private-app, and data tiers across two AZs. Every child is disjoint; the peered on-prem /16 is out of scope and must never overlap. The suspect edge is the peering boundary where a duplicate range silently drops traffic.

storyboard.say: Start with the parent: one /16 block, 10.20.0.0/16, giving you 16 host bits and about 65 thousand addresses to carve.
First carve: a Public /20 for internet-facing subnets — the /20 fixes 20 network bits, leaving a clean, right-sized slice.
Next, two App tiers, one per availability zone — App AZ-a and App AZ-b, each its own /20 so failure of one AZ never takes both.
The Data tier gets a tighter /22 — fewer hosts by design, since databases need far less address space than app fleets.
The invariant: every child is disjoint. Public, both App zones, and Data must never overlap under the same parent.
Now the suspect edge — a peering route to on-prem 10.10.0.0/16, a separate space that is out of scope and must never overlap ours.
Here's the trap: pick a duplicate range on either side and the router sees two identical destinations and silently drops half the traffic.
The lesson: this outage is an address-space decision made months earlier — plan disjoint CIDRs up front, before any route is written.

cidr-and-subnets.text: The senior tell is aligning every subnet on its prefix boundary and leaving deliberate gaps to grow into. cidr-and-subnets.question: A reviewer challenges your plan: 'Prove these two subnets can't collide when we peer.' Which answer actually proves it?
options: "They're in different availability zones, so they're isolated."
"10.20.16.0/20 covers 10.20.16.0–10.20.31.255 and 10.20.32.0/20 covers 10.20.32.0–10.20.47.255 — the ranges don't touch, and neither overlaps the peered 10.10.0.0/16."
"They have different names and security groups, so traffic is separated."
"I used a /20 for both, and /20s are always safe."
cidr-and-subnets.explanation: Overlap is a property of address ranges, not names, AZs, or security groups. Only option 2 states the concrete first/last address of each block and shows the ranges are disjoint from each other and from the peer — the exact evidence a routing table needs. AZs, names, and 'a /20 is safe' are the false-confidence answers that survive review and then drop traffic in production.

cidr-and-subnets.intro: Prove your CIDR plan holds — no eyeballing:
items: Run ipcalc (or the equivalent) on every subnet and confirm HostMin/HostMax match what you wrote — a boundary off by one octet is an overlap waiting to happen.

Overlap-check the parent and every child against every peered VPC and on-prem range: no two ranges may share a single address.
Confirm each subnet starts on its own prefix boundary — an unaligned start (e.g. a /20 beginning at .17.0) silently overlaps its neighbor.
Trace one packet: from a public LB to an app host to the data tier — does a route or NetworkPolicy exist for each hop, or does the split forbid it? Name which.

nat-and-routes.text: A production service is green for you and half the office, and a hard 502 for the other half — same build, same region. The team has spent two hours rereading the request handler while the real culprit is a route that only exists one way and a NAT table that dropped the return packets.

This is lesson 2 of Addressing, Routing & Load Balancing — you can already reason about addresses and paths, now you trace failure across them. NAT and routes decide whether a packet even reaches your service and whether its reply can get home, which is exactly the layer teams skip when they debug application code for a network problem.

nat-and-routes.prompt: A service works for clients in Subnet A but times out for clients in Subnet B. The app logs show NO errors for the Subnet B requests at all. Where is the failure — and why is 'no errors' the loudest clue? Answer before reading on.
nat-and-routes.reveal: Silence upstream of your code is the tell. If the app never logged the request, the packet never arrived — the failure is a hop BEFORE the application: a missing return route for Subnet B, a NAT rule that only rewrites A's source, or a NetworkPolicy that admits A and drops B. Route asymmetry is the classic trap: the request reaches you, your reply takes a path with no NAT translation, and the client sees a timeout while your server sees a clean, successful handler run. Both 'sides' are telling the truth; they're describing different halves of the path.

nat-and-routes.intro: Walking the path with inspection hooks. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
nat-and-routes.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
HOST=service.example.com

# Hop 1 — DNS: does the name resolve, and to the VIP you expect?
dig +short "$HOST"            # expect: 10.20.0.5  (the service VIP)

# Hop 2/3 — Route & NAT: from the FAILING client's subnet,
# does a route exist and does the reply come back?
ip route get 10.20.0.5        # expect a route via the NAT gateway, not 'unreachable'
curl -v --max-time 5 "https://$HOST/health"   # timeout here + app-side 200 => asymmetric return / lost NAT conntrack

# Hop 4 — TLS trust: is the cert chain valid FROM THIS client?
openssl s_client -connect "$HOST:443" -servername "$HOST" </dev/null 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'Verify return code|subject='   # expect: Verify return code: 0 (ok)

# Hop 5 — Policy: is the failing client's CIDR actually admitted?
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-frontends   # expect the client's source CIDR in an ingress 'from' block
steps: Prove DNS first: dig +short returns the answer with zero noise. Wrong or empty VIP = the failure is name resolution; stop here, everything downstream is chasing a ghost.

Route + NAT together: ip route get shows the egress path from THIS host; a working forward with a curl timeout is the asymmetric-route / dropped-conntrack signature. This is the hop app logs cannot see.

TLS trust from the client: 'Verify return code: 0' means trusted. A non-zero code that only some clients hit is a missing intermediate cert or a client that lacks the CA — a trust fact, not an app bug.

Policy is the last silent dropper: kubectl describe networkpolicy shows exactly which source CIDRs are admitted. If the failing subnet is absent, the drop happens before your pod — the app never logs it.
Fail fast, in order: set -euo pipefail plus top-down order = the FIRST hop that misbehaves is the cause. You isolate signal from noise by construction, not by guessing.

storyboard.say: Client B in Subnet B starts the request by asking the DNS resolver to turn the service name into an address.
DNS returns the service VIP, and the request enters the router, which consults its route table to decide the forward path.
The router hands off to the NAT gateway, which SNATs the source so the return traffic knows how to find its way back.
Translated packets traverse the firewall, and the NetworkPolicy admits them into the service pod, which processes the request.
First silent trap: if Subnet B is not in the allow-CIDR, the policy drops Client B outright while other subnets sail through.
The reply exits through an asymmetric route straight back to the router, skipping the NAT gateway entirely.
Second trap: with no reverse translation, the return packet's address is wrong, so it never reaches Client B.
Server logs success, client sees a timeout: the failure lives on one hop, route and NAT, not in the app code.

load-balancer-modes.text: Half your users hit the checkout fine; the other half get intermittent 502s, and the app team has spent four hours re-reading code that works. The real fault is the load balancer: it is running L4 pass-through, the health check probes a TCP port that is open while the app behind it is returning errors — so the LB keeps sending traffic into a dead backend.

This lesson lives in Addressing, Routing and Load Balancing, right after routing: once packets reach the right network, the load balancer decides which backend answers and how the reply gets home. The mode you pick (L4 vs L7, SNAT vs DSR) changes what you can observe, what health checks can catch, and where 'reachable for some, broken for others' comes from.

load-balancer-modes.prompt: "Users on one region get 502s intermittently; the app is healthy." Before blaming the app — what should you check about the load balancer FIRST? Answer before reading on.
load-balancer-modes.reveal: Check the LB's mode and its health check, not the app. An L4 (transport) LB only proves a TCP port is open — a backend can accept connections while returning 5xx, so L4 health checks pass on a broken node and keep routing to it. Move the check to L7 (HTTP GET /health expecting 200) and the dead backend drops out. The 'oh': the LB was healthy about the wrong layer. The mode decides which failures are even visible.

load-balancer-modes.intro: Proving the mode from the outside — dig, curl, openssl. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
load-balancer-modes.code:
# 1. Resolve the VIP — is it one address or many (DNS-level LB)?
dig +short service.example.com
# 203.0.113.10   <- single VIP => balancing happens at the LB, not DNS

# 2. Is TLS terminated AT the LB (L7) or passed through (L4)?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject
# issuer=... Amazon RSA ...  subject=CN=service.example.com  <- LB cert => L7 terminates here

# 3. Does the LB route on HTTP content, and which backend answered?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
# > GET /health HTTP/2
# < HTTP/2 200
# < x-served-by: backend-a        <- L7 routing header proves content-aware LB
# < x-lb-mode: round_robin        <- confirms the algorithm actually in use

# 4. Confirm the broken backend is actually being evicted (L7 health check)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --resolve service.example.com:443:203.0.113.11 https://service.example.com/health
# 503  <- backend-b is unhealthy; an L7 check drops it, an L4 :443-open check would not
steps: Rule out DNS-level balancing: One A record means the LB itself splits traffic. Many rotating records would mean DNS round-robin is a co-conspirator — a different mode entirely.

L4 vs L7: who owns the cert?: If the certificate subject is your LB / cloud provider, TLS terminates at the LB — that is L7. A pass-through cert (your origin's own leaf, no LB in the chain) points to L4.
Content routing + the mode header: An x-served-by / x-lb-mode header is only possible if the LB reads HTTP — direct proof of L7. Record which backend answered so you can tie a 5xx to a specific node.

Force the suspect backend: --resolve pins the request to one backend IP. A 503 here that the VIP never shows means the L7 health check is correctly evicting it — the exact evidence an L4 check could not produce.

load-balancer-modes.title: A mode is a layer + a return path — not a product
load-balancer-modes.text: L4 balances by IP/port (fast, blind to HTTP); L7 balances by request content (routes, cookies, headers — and real HTTP health checks). Orthogonally, the reply either returns through the LB (SNAT) or straight to the client (Direct Server Return). Constraint picks the mode; the mode decides what you can observe and repair.

storyboard.say: A user hits checkout: the client first resolves the name in DNS, then sends its request to the load balancer's virtual IP.
The load balancer is the decision point: it must choose which backend answers, and it picks candidates using its health check.
Backend A is healthy, so the health check keeps it and the load balancer freely forwards live checkout traffic to it.
Here is the suspect edge: Backend B returns 5xx, yet an L4 check only sees an open TCP port, so it keeps a broken server.
L7 changes what you can observe: it terminates TLS and runs a real GET /health, sees the 5xx, and evicts Backend B.
The reply path is the other choice: SNAT returns through the balancer, or Direct Server Return sends the response straight home.
So intermittent 502s aren't app bugs: the mode picks what health checks can catch, and that's where 'broken for some' is born.

load-balancer-modes.title: Proving the mode from the outside — dig, curl, openssl
load-balancer-modes.subtitle: The inspection-hook block of the decision packet: three commands that turn 'I think it's L7' into observable evidence.
load-balancer-modes.code:
# 1. Resolve the VIP — is it one address or many (DNS-level LB)?
dig +short service.example.com
# 203.0.113.10   <- single VIP => balancing happens at the LB, not DNS

# 2. Is TLS terminated AT the LB (L7) or passed through (L4)?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject
# issuer=... Amazon RSA ...  subject=CN=service.example.com  <- LB cert => L7 terminates here

# 3. Does the LB route on HTTP content, and which backend answered?
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
# > GET /health HTTP/2
# < HTTP/2 200
# < x-served-by: backend-a        <- L7 routing header proves content-aware LB
# < x-lb-mode: round_robin        <- confirms the algorithm actually in use

# 4. Confirm the broken backend is actually being evicted (L7 health check)
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" --resolve service.example.com:443:203.0.113.11 https://service.example.com/health
# 503  <- backend-b is unhealthy; an L7 check drops it, an L4 :443-open check would not

steps.label: Rule out DNS-level balancing
steps.note: One A record means the LB itself splits traffic. Many rotating records would mean DNS round-robin is a co-conspirator — a different mode entirely.

steps.label: L4 vs L7: who owns the cert?
steps.note: If the certificate subject is your LB / cloud provider, TLS terminates at the LB — that is L7. A pass-through cert (your origin's own leaf, no LB in the chain) points to L4.

steps.label: Content routing + the mode header
steps.note: An x-served-by / x-lb-mode header is only possible if the LB reads HTTP — direct proof of L7. Record which backend answered so you can tie a 5xx to a specific node.

steps.label: Force the suspect backend
steps.note: --resolve pins the request to one backend IP. A 503 here that the VIP never shows means the L7 health check is correctly evicting it — the exact evidence an L4 check could not produce.

load-balancer-modes.text: Standards grounding: an L4 load balancer operates at OSI transport (TCP per RFC 793/9293, UDP per RFC 768) and cannot see HTTP; an L7 balancer terminates TLS and reads the request, which is why only L7 supports path/host routing and real HTTP health checks (against the HTTP semantics defined in RFC 9110). Note: 'L4/L7' is industry layering terminology, not an RFC 9110 term. Direct Server Return (DSR) exists because at high scale, forcing every reply back through the LB (SNAT) makes it the bottleneck — DSR lets backends answer clients directly, at the cost of the LB no longer seeing return traffic. The mode is a throughput-vs-observability trade, and you must name which side the constraint puts you on.

load-balancer-modes.question: Reviewer challenge: you claim 'the load balancer is L7 and evicts unhealthy backends,' but some clients still hit 502s. Which evidence actually proves the mode is doing its job?
options: The LB dashboard shows all backends 'green'.
A TCP health check on port 443 passes for every backend.
curl -v against the VIP returns 200 with an x-served-by header, AND a --resolve request pinned to the suspect backend returns 503 while the VIP never routes to it.
The application team confirms their code is unchanged since last week.
load-balancer-modes.explanation: Only option 3 is inspectable and falsifiable: the x-served-by header proves the LB reads HTTP (L7), and the pinned --resolve 503 that the VIP never serves proves the health check is genuinely evicting the bad backend. A green dashboard (1) and a passing TCP check (2) are exactly the blind signals an L4 mode gives on a 5xx node; 'code unchanged' (4) is the trap that keeps teams debugging the wrong layer.

proxy-and-cdn-path.text: The deploy went clean, but support is flooded: half your users load the site instantly, the other half get a spinning white screen or a scary certificate warning. Three engineers are already diffing last night's application PR — while the real break is a stale CDN edge serving a cert for the wrong hostname to one region.

A proxy/CDN sits between the client and your origin, so a request now survives DNS resolution, a CDN edge, TLS termination, and origin routing before your code runs. 'Reachable for some, broken for others' is almost never the app — it is one hop on that path behaving differently by region, resolver, or cache.

proxy-and-cdn-path.prompt: Users in one region get a TLS certificate error; users elsewhere are fine. The app is byte-identical for everyone. Where do you look first — and why is 'read the application logs' the wrong first move? Answer before reading on.
proxy-and-cdn-path.reveal: TLS terminates at the CDN edge, not your origin — so a cert error means a specific edge (or its SNI/hostname config) is wrong, and your origin logs will show nothing because the request never reached it. The right first move is `openssl s_client -connect <edge-ip>:443 -servername your.host` against the failing region's edge and a healthy one, then compare the presented certificate chain. The path forks at the edge; the app is a red herring by construction.

proxy-and-cdn-path.intro: Tracing the path with real inspection hooks. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
proxy-and-cdn-path.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md :: evidence commands
set -euo pipefail
HOST=service.example.com

# 1. DNS: which edge IP does each region's resolver return?
dig +short $HOST @1.1.1.1        # region-A resolver
dig +short $HOST @8.8.8.8        # region-B resolver (compare answers)

# 2. TLS: what cert does the FAILING edge actually present?
openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.10:443 -servername $HOST </dev/null \
  2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -dates

# 3. HTTP: force the request through a specific edge, watch the exchange
curl -v --resolve $HOST:443:203.0.113.10 https://$HOST/health

# 4. Origin policy: can the edge even reach the backend pool?
kubectl describe networkpolicy origin-allow -n edge-ingress
steps: Pin the host: One variable, so every hook targets the same name the client used — no accidental host drift between commands.
DNS divergence first: GeoDNS can hand different edge IPs to different resolvers. If the two `dig` answers differ, you have already localized the fork to DNS before touching TLS.

What cert does the edge REALLY present: openssl s_client against the failing edge IP shows the subject + validity dates. A wrong subject or an expired date here explains the whole 'some clients' TLS error — origin logs never saw it.
curl --resolve pins the edge: Bypasses your own resolver to force the request through the SUSPECT edge IP. `-v` prints the TLS handshake and response headers so you see exactly where it dies.
Rule out origin policy: If TLS and DNS pass, the break may be edge→origin: a NetworkPolicy denying the proxy. This is the hop teams skip — and then blame the app.

storyboard.say: The deploy was clean, but half your users load instantly and the other half get a spinning white screen or a scary cert warning.
The request doesn't hit your code first. It's an ordered path of hops, so trace it in order instead of blaming the app PR.
First hop: the client resolves the host through GeoDNS, which hands back a different edge IP depending on the caller's region.
Now the client opens a TLS handshake to that edge. For region A it fails, because the edge serves a stale cert for the wrong host.
The CDN edge is the diverging hop: healthy regions terminate TLS and pass, region A breaks before a byte reaches origin.
Only on a cache miss does the edge fetch from the origin proxy, which is subject to NetworkPolicy before forwarding to the backend.
The backend stays out of scope until the path is proven. Confirm the diverging hop with dig, curl, and openssl before touching code.

proxy-and-cdn-path.text: The senior tell in a path incident: distinguish an application SYMPTOM (500, blank page, spinner) from a network CAUSE (name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or policy). Every hook you run should be able to return 'this hop is fine' and move the search forward — a check that can only confirm your favorite theory is theater, not a trace.

proxy-and-cdn-path.question: A reviewer challenges your packet: 'How do I know the CDN edge is the break and not the backend?' Which evidence actually proves it?
options: The application error rate spiked in Grafana at the same time as the reports.
`curl -v --resolve host:443:<failing-edge-ip>` dies in the TLS handshake, while the same curl against a healthy edge returns 200 — and origin access logs show zero requests from the failing region.
You restarted the backend pods and some users recovered.
The on-call engineer is 'pretty sure' it's the edge because that's what broke last time.
proxy-and-cdn-path.explanation: Option 2 is inspectable and falsifiable: the handshake dies at the edge for the failing IP but succeeds at a healthy one, AND the origin never logged the request — so the break is provably upstream of the backend. A correlated Grafana spike (1) shows symptom timing, not the causal hop; a lucky restart (3) is a coincidence with no path evidence; 'last time' (4) is a hunch. The packet must point at the exact hop with command output another reviewer can replay.

vpc-vnet-design.outcome: Take one real (or realistic) cloud service that is reachable from some clients but fails for others, and write the VPC/VNet decision packet: the boundary you are drawing (CIDR blocks, subnets, route tables, security groups, NetworkPolicy), the one non-negotiable constraint, the rejected topology, and the exact path-trace that proves reachability — before you touch application code.
vpc-vnet-design.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with a constraint table, the selected VPC/VNet topology, one rejected option and why it fails under the boundary, a dig/curl/openssl verification trail, a named failure trigger, and one reviewer objection answered. A peer can replay the trace and reach the same reachable/blocked verdict without you narrating.
vpc-vnet-design.unlock: Your packet names the boundary and ownership, attaches at least one inspection-hook output (dig / curl -v / openssl s_client / kubectl describe networkpolicy), and states what result would make the decision invalid.
vpc-vnet-design.doNotClaim: Do not claim the service is 'reachable' because it works from your laptop. Your laptop is one client on one path. Reachability is a property of a specific source, a specific route table, and a specific policy — prove it per boundary, or you have proven nothing.

vpc-vnet-design.text: The service returns 200 from the bastion, 200 from your laptop over VPN, and a dead 28-second hang from the new EKS pod in the private subnet — and three engineers are already rewriting the app's retry logic. Nobody has run dig. The failure was never in the code; it was a missing route between two subnets nobody drew a boundary around.

A VPC/VNet is the boundary every cloud request crosses before your code ever runs — CIDR ranges, subnets, route tables, security groups, and NetworkPolicy decide who can even reach you. This is lesson 1 of Cloud & Kubernetes Networking because every later topic (load balancers, ingress, service mesh) lives inside the address space and routing you design here.

vpc-vnet-design.prompt: Two teams pick a VPC CIDR. Team A picks 10.0.0.0/16. Team B, on a different account, also picks 10.0.0.0/16 — both 'work' in isolation. What breaks, and when? Answer before reading on.
vpc-vnet-design.reveal: Nothing breaks — until you peer them. VPC peering and Transit Gateway refuse overlapping CIDRs, and even if routing 'accepts' it, the return path is ambiguous: a packet for 10.0.1.5 has two homes. The failure is invisible in isolation and catastrophic at integration, which is exactly why CIDR is a design-time boundary decision, not a runtime one. 'It works in my VPC' is the network equivalent of 'it works on my machine' — reachability is a property of the whole address plan, not one island.

vpc-vnet-design.intro: The decision packet + the trace that proves it. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
vpc-vnet-design.code:
## VPC/VNet Design Decision Packet
# Constraint: no daytime downtime; private subnets must NOT reach the internet directly
# Boundary: VPC 10.20.0.0/16 | public 10.20.0.0/20 | private 10.20.16.0/20 | db 10.20.32.0/20
# Selected: 3-tier (public ALB) -> (private app) -> (isolated db), egress via NAT only
# Rejected: single flat public subnet -> pods get public IPs -> violates the constraint

## Verification trail (run per boundary, not just from the bastion)
$ dig +short app.svc.internal            # 10.20.16.9  -> DNS resolves inside VPC
$ curl -v --max-time 5 https://app.svc.internal/health
  * Connected to 10.20.16.9 port 443      # SG allows 443 from ALB SG
  < HTTP/2 200                            # reachable on the intended path
$ curl -v --max-time 5 https://10.20.32.5:5432   # from the app pod -> RDS
  * connect to 10.20.32.5 timed out       # <-- FAILURE: no route table entry
$ kubectl describe networkpolicy app-egress -n prod
  Egress: to 10.20.32.0/20 :5432          # policy allows it; the ROUTE does not

## Failure trigger:  reachable from ALB, times out to DB  =>  missing db-subnet route
## Reviewer objection:  "proven, or merely described?"  ->  attach the curl timeout + route table diff
steps: Constraint before topology: Name the non-negotiable first — 'no direct internet from private subnets'. It must rule out at least one plausible design (the flat public subnet), or it is decoration.

Selected vs rejected: The 3-tier boundary is the choice; the flat single-subnet is the rejected option and WHY it fails under the constraint. Recording the rejection is what makes the packet inspectable.

dig — name resolution first: Trace the path in order: DNS before TLS before routing. A resolvable name that still times out proves the failure is downstream of DNS — you just eliminated a whole branch.
curl -v — the reachable path: 443 returns 200 from the ALB's security group. This boundary is proven reachable. Do NOT stop here — one green path is not the whole packet.

The failing boundary: curl from the pod to RDS times out. Same code, different source, different route table — the classic 'debugs app code while the real issue is routing' failure this lesson exists to kill.
Policy allows, route denies: kubectl shows NetworkPolicy permits egress to :5432 — so the block is NOT policy, it is a missing route-table entry. Separating policy from routing is the expert move.

Failure trigger + objection: State the exact trigger (reachable from ALB, times out to DB) and answer the reviewer's 'proven or described?' with the attached curl timeout and route diff. That attachment is the difference between a claim and evidence.

vpc-vnet-design.title: A VPC design is an address plan + a reachability boundary — not a pile of subnets
vpc-vnet-design.text: Draw non-overlapping CIDR, split public/private subnets by trust, and make every allowed path explicit: route table, security group, NetworkPolicy. The invariant — a request is reachable only if you can trace it end to end. Anything you can't trace, you can't trust.

vpc-vnet-design.title: The VPC reachability path — where a private request lives or dies
vpc-vnet-design.subtitle: A client → ALB → private subnet → pod, crossing four boundaries: route table, security group, NAT for egress, and NetworkPolicy. The suspect edge (private subnet → RDS with no route) is marked; the blast radius is 'reachable from public, blocked from private'. On-prem VPN and peered analytics VPC are deliberately out of scope.

storyboard.say: A client opens a request on 443 to the public ALB, the one door into this VPC that faces the internet.
The ALB forwards inbound traffic to the security group, the stateful firewall that decides who may reach the pod.
The security group allows 443 through to the app pod living in the private subnet, so the request finally reaches your code.
For outbound DNS and TLS the pod routes through the NAT gateway, the only sanctioned path to the internet from a private subnet.
Here is where it dies: the pod tries Postgres on 5432, but the private subnet's route table has no route to RDS, so it hangs 28 seconds.
The blast radius is telling: reachable from public over the ALB, blocked from private toward the store. It was never the app's retry code.
And NetworkPolicy holds the invariant: the analytics VPC must not leak in. If you can't trace a path end to end, you can't trust it.

vpc-vnet-design.text: The senior tell: a strong networking answer distinguishes application symptoms from network causes. When a request 'hangs', the amateur reads their own code; the pro traces the path — DNS lookup, IP route, TLS trust, then HTTP — and finds the layer that actually broke. vpc-vnet-design.question: Your reviewer says: 'You claim the payments service is reachable from the workers — prove it, don't describe it.' Which response is the evidence they want?
options: 'The security group allows 443 and the NetworkPolicy permits egress, so it must be reachable.'
A dig showing the name resolves, a curl -v from a worker pod showing the 200 (or the exact timeout), and the route-table entry that carries that path — attached to the packet.

service-discovery.text: The service is green in one region and throwing connection errors in another, and three engineers are already rewriting the retry logic — nobody has run a single dig. The staff engineer asks one question — "is the name even resolving to the right IP from the pod that fails?" — and the room goes quiet.

In Kubernetes the same Service name resolves differently depending on namespace, cluster DNS, TLS trust, and NetworkPolicy — so "works for me, fails for them" is the default, not the exception. This lesson turns that asymmetry into a traced path with proof at each hop, the packet you carry into the module capstone.

service-discovery.prompt: A service is reachable from client A but times out from client B after a config change. Where do you look FIRST — the application code, or somewhere else? Decide before reading on.
service-discovery.reveal: Not the code — the path, in order: DNS lookup, IP route, TLS trust, then HTTP. The failure is asymmetric, and application code is identical for A and B, so it cannot be the cause on its own. The senior move is to run the SAME dig / curl -v from inside pod A and pod B and diff them: if the name resolves to different IPs, or one gets a TLS trust error the other does not, you have crossed off the entire application layer with two commands. Debugging the code first feels like progress while quietly assuming the one thing the asymmetry rules out.

service-discovery.intro: The packet's evidence section — one hook at a time. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
service-discovery.code:
## Constraint
# Failing: client pod B (ns=frontend). Working: pod A (ns=admin). No daytime downtime.

## Hop 1 — DNS resolution (from the FAILING pod)
dig orders.backend.svc.cluster.local +short   # B: NXDOMAIN | A: 10.96.42.7
# -> B resolves nothing. Suspect: search-domain / namespace, not the app.

## Hop 2 — NetworkPolicy (does egress even leave pod B?)
kubectl describe networkpolicy -n frontend
# -> default-deny egress; no rule allows ns=backend. B is blocked at the policy.

## Hop 3 — TLS trust (rule OUT cert asymmetry)
openssl s_client -connect orders.backend:443 -servername orders.backend </dev/null
# -> A: verify return:0 (cert SAN matches). Not a trust failure.

## Hop 4 — HTTP (only reached once 1+2 pass)
curl -v https://orders.backend/health   # A: 200 | B: could not resolve host

## Cause: NetworkPolicy default-deny egress in ns=frontend blocks B->backend.
## Rejected: "app retry bug" — identical code in A and B; ruled out by the diff.
## Invalidates this: if dig succeeds AND policy allows AND B still fails -> reopen at TLS/HTTP.
steps: State the asymmetry as a constraint: Failing pod, working pod, and the non-negotiable (no daytime downtime). The diff between A and B IS the diagnostic — it rules out anything identical across both.
Hop 1: dig from the FAILING pod: Run dig inside pod B, not from your laptop. NXDOMAIN vs a real ClusterIP tells you resolution broke before routing ever mattered. This is the cheapest disqualifier.
Hop 2: kubectl describe networkpolicy: A default-deny egress with no allow rule to the backend namespace blocks B silently — the app sees a timeout, the network saw a policy drop.
Hop 3: openssl s_client rules OUT trust: verify return:0 means the cert SAN matched — a passing hook is pure profit, it permanently eliminates the TLS branch for pod A.
Hop 4: curl -v only after 1+2 pass: 'could not resolve host' confirms the failure never reached HTTP. The app layer was never in play.

Cause, rejected option, and invalidation: Name the layer, record the ruled-out explanation, and state exactly what result would reopen the case. That last line is what makes the packet inspectable instead of a story.
