service-discovery.title: The service-discovery path — where "some clients fail" hides
service-discovery.subtitle: Pod B's request crosses four gates before it reaches the Service. The failure lives on one edge (CoreDNS resolution or the NetworkPolicy), not in the app. Payments and the app's business logic are deliberately out of scope.

storyboard.say: Same service, green in one region, throwing connection errors in another. Before touching retry logic, trace where Pod B's request actually breaks.
Gate one is DNS. Pod B asks CoreDNS to resolve the Service name, and CoreDNS hands back a ClusterIP.
Namespace and cluster DNS decide what that name means, so the very first hop can already return a different IP for the failing pod.
Gate two is the NetworkPolicy. Pod B's egress and the Service's ingress must both allow the connection, or it dies silently before routing.
If allowed, the Service selects its EndpointSlice and that slice routes to a live Backend Pod IP.
Gate three is trust. Pod B verifies the certificate SAN against the Backend Pod before it will speak.
Only gate four sends HTTP, once trust holds. The failure lives on one edge, DNS or NetworkPolicy, never in the app.

ingress-and-services.doNotClaim: Do not claim you 'debugged the ingress' if your only evidence is that a curl worked from your laptop. One client succeeding proves nothing about the client that fails — route asymmetry, split-horizon DNS, and per-namespace NetworkPolicy all pass from the happy path. Proof lives on the FAILING path, not the working one.

ingress-and-services.text: The service is green on every dashboard, half the customers can reach it, and three engineers are already rewriting the handler that 'must be dropping requests.' Nobody has run a single dig from the client that fails — so nobody yet knows the app was never the problem.

In Kubernetes a request crosses DNS, IP routing, TLS trust, HTTP semantics, the Service's kube-proxy hop, the Ingress router, and NetworkPolicy before it ever reaches your code. 'Works for some, fails for others' is the signature of a network-path fault — and this packet is where you prove which layer, with evidence a reviewer can replay.

ingress-and-services.prompt: A Service is reachable from pods in namespace A but times out from namespace B. Same image, same replicas, same Ingress. Where do you look first — the application, or somewhere else? Decide before reading on.
ingress-and-services.reveal: Not the application — identical code cannot behave differently by caller namespace. That asymmetry is the tell: a default-deny NetworkPolicy in namespace B (or a missing ingress rule allowing A but not B) is silently dropping the connection before HTTP begins. 'kubectl describe networkpolicy' in B settles it in seconds; re-reading the handler would burn the night. When the SAME service answers some callers and not others, the variable is the PATH, never the code.

ingress-and-services.intro: The decision packet: tracing the failing layer with real hooks. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
ingress-and-services.code:
## Constraint
# No daytime downtime on the checkout path; fix must not restart the Ingress.

## Layer trace (external client = OK, internal ns B = FAIL)
# L1 DNS  — resolves to the LB, so name resolution is NOT the fault:
dig +short api.example.com            # 203.0.113.10  (external)
dig +short api.example.com @10.96.0.10 # 10.100.4.7   (in-cluster ClusterIP)

# L3/L4 route + L6 TLS — external path is clean end to end:
curl -v https://api.example.com/health            # < HTTP/2 200
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep 'Verify return'
#   Verify return code: 0 (ok)   → cert chain trusted, TLS is NOT the fault

# L7 from the FAILING client — hangs, no HTTP response at all:
kubectl -n ns-b run probe --image=curlimages/curl --rm -it -- \
  curl -sS --max-time 5 http://api.svc.cluster.local/health   # timeout, exit 28

# Policy — the drop: ns B is absent from the ingress allow-list:
kubectl describe networkpolicy api-allow -n api-ns
#   Allowing ingress from: NamespaceSelector team=a   (ns B has team=b)

## Selected approach: add team=b to the NetworkPolicy from-selector (hot-apply, no restart)
## Rejected approach: loosen to Allow-All ingress — removes the isolation the constraint depends on
## Failure trigger: any client whose namespace label is not in the from-selector
## Verification: re-run the ns-b probe → expect HTTP 200; capture before/after
steps: Constraint first: Name the non-negotiable (no daytime restart) BEFORE any fix — it will rule out at least one option. This is the move that separates a decision from a guess.
L1 — clear DNS: Resolve from BOTH sides. External returns the LB, in-cluster returns the ClusterIP — both resolve, so name resolution is eliminated, not assumed innocent.
L3–L6 — clear route + TLS: curl -v proves routing + HTTP on the happy path; openssl 'Verify return code: 0' proves the cert chain is trusted. Two layers crossed off with two commands.

L7 — reproduce from the FAILING client: Run the probe from INSIDE ns B. Exit 28 (timeout) with no HTTP status means the connection dies below L7 — the app is never reached. This is the load-bearing evidence.
The drop is named: describe networkpolicy shows the from-selector allows team=a only. ns B is labelled team=b → default-deny drops it. Cause proven at the policy layer, not inferred.

Decide + reject + verify: Selected: add team=b to the from-selector (hot-applies, honours the no-restart constraint). Rejected: Allow-All — it works but destroys the isolation the constraint exists to protect.

ingress-and-services.text: A request is DNS → route → TLS → HTTP → Service → Ingress → NetworkPolicy. Walk it in order, separate what you can observe from what you infer, and prove the failing layer. Asymmetry (some clients, not others) means the cause is on the path, not in the code.

ingress-and-services.title: The request path: where 'reachable for some, broken for others' hides
ingress-and-services.subtitle: External client → DNS → Ingress (TLS terminates) → Service (kube-proxy) → Pod. NetworkPolicy gates the Service edge; the internal client's request is silently dropped there — the app is never reached.

the drop point — NetworkPolicy denies ns B

storyboard.say: Start where the packet starts. The external client resolves the hostname through DNS, which hands back the load balancer IP.
From the LB IP the request hits the Ingress, TLS terminates cleanly, and it's routed onward to the Service.
The Service's kube-proxy picks endpoints, but NetworkPolicy sits on that edge and decides who is actually allowed through.
For traffic from namespace A the policy says allow, so the packet reaches the Pod and the app answers. Dashboards go green.
Now the other client: an internal caller in namespace B makes an in-cluster call to the same Service.
Namespace B isn't in the policy's from list, so the packet is silently dropped here. The app is never reached.
That asymmetry is the tell: some clients pass, others don't. The fault is on the path, not in the handler code.

networkpolicy-boundaries.outcome: Take a real (or realistic) Kubernetes service that is reachable from some clients but blocked for others after a NetworkPolicy change, and write the decision packet: the allowed-vs-denied path, the constraint (deny-by-default namespace), the policy you would ship, the policy you rejected, the failure that reappears, and the exact dig/curl/kubectl evidence that proves it.
networkpolicy-boundaries.proof: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md with: context, the suspect edge on the path (namespace ingress on port 8080), selected policy, rejected policy, expected failure trigger, verification via `kubectl describe networkpolicy` + `curl -v` from an allowed and a denied pod, one reviewer objection answered, and a transfer note. A reviewer can replay the deny and watch your policy flip it to allow.
networkpolicy-boundaries.unlock: Your packet names the constraint before the policy, shows the exact allow/deny path, and attaches at least one inspection-hook output (dig, curl, openssl, or kubectl describe networkpolicy).
networkpolicy-boundaries.doNotClaim: Do not claim the boundary is 'proven' because the manifest applied cleanly. `kubectl apply` succeeding says the YAML parsed, not that the right traffic is allowed and the wrong traffic is denied. Proof is a curl from a pod that SHOULD reach it succeeding, AND a curl from a pod that should NOT reach it timing out — both observed, not assumed.

networkpolicy-boundaries.text: The deploy went out at 14:02, and by 14:05 the payments team is paging: their checkout pods get connection-refused to your service, but your own smoke test from the same namespace passes green. The app didn't change. A deny-by-default NetworkPolicy landed on the namespace and quietly cut every ingress you never explicitly allowed.

In Kubernetes, a NetworkPolicy is a boundary that decides which pods may reach which pods — and the instant one deny-by-default policy selects a namespace, every allow becomes something you must state on purpose. This is release/review risk: the code is innocent, the boundary is the incident.

networkpolicy-boundaries.prompt: Your service works from your own pods but fails from the payments namespace after a policy change. The instinct is to open the app logs and hunt the 500. Before you do — what does that instinct cost you here? Answer before reading on.
networkpolicy-boundaries.reveal: There is no 500 to find. A denied NetworkPolicy connection never reaches your app — the SYN is dropped at the pod network, so your service logs nothing and your traces are empty. Reading app logs is searching the one place the evidence cannot be. The signal lives one layer down: `kubectl describe networkpolicy`, and a `curl -v` from the payments pod that hangs on 'Trying 10.x.x.x…' and times out. Empty app logs + a client-side timeout is the fingerprint of a policy deny, not a bug.

networkpolicy-boundaries.intro: The gold artifact: a deny-by-default policy plus one scoped allow. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
networkpolicy-boundaries.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-default-deny-plus-payments
  namespace: api
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              role: payments
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
# Verify (the proof, not the apply):
#   kubectl describe networkpolicy api-default-deny-plus-payments -n api
#   kubectl exec -n payments deploy/checkout -- curl -v --max-time 5 http://api.api.svc:8080/health   # MUST pass
#   kubectl exec -n default   deploy/scratch  -- curl -v --max-time 5 http://api.api.svc:8080/health   # MUST time out
steps: The boundary target: podSelector app=api scopes the policy to your service's pods. This is the surface you are drawing a boundary around — get it wrong and you protect the wrong pods.

Ingress-only = deny-by-default inbound: Listing Ingress in policyTypes flips the default: any inbound not matched below is now DENIED. This single line is what caused the payments outage — and what you're now stating on purpose.

The one allow, keyed to a label: Allow ingress FROM pods labeled role=payments. Label-scoped, not an IP or CIDR — pods get new IPs on every reschedule, so a CIDR allow rots. This is the rejected-option boundary made concrete.
Scope the port too: Allow only TCP 8080. An allow with no ports opens every port on the pod — a quiet over-grant a reviewer will catch.
Proof #1 — the allowed path passes: curl from a payments pod MUST return 200. If it hangs, your podSelector label doesn't match the real pod labels — the classic silent miss.

Proof #2 — the denied path times out: curl from an unlisted namespace MUST time out, not refuse. A timeout (dropped SYN) is the signature of a working deny; a fast connection-refused means the policy isn't selecting the pod at all.
networkpolicy-boundaries.commonMistake: Reopens the outage by deleting the boundary

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: A NetworkPolicy boundary is deny-by-default plus every allow stated on purpose
networkpolicy-boundaries.text: The moment a policy selects pods, unlisted ingress is denied. The boundary is correct only when you can name who is allowed, who is denied, and show both — a curl that should pass passing, and a curl that should fail timing out.

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: The blocked path: where the deny happens, and where the repair lands
networkpolicy-boundaries.subtitle: Payments pod → your service on port 8080. The deny-by-default policy on the api namespace drops ingress from unlabeled sources (the failure path, red). The fix is a targeted ingress allow keyed to the payments pod label (the repair path, green). DNS and TLS are on the path but are NOT the cause — marked muted so you don't chase them.

legend.label: failure path — policy drops the SYN, app logs nothing
repair path — a scoped ingress allow, keyed to the pod label
on the path but NOT the cause (DNS/TLS/same-ns) — don't chase

storyboard.say: The payments pod resolves your service name fine — CoreDNS answers, so DNS is not the incident. Don't chase it.
The payments pod opens a SYN to your api service on port 8080. This is the real request path we care about.
A deny-by-default NetworkPolicy now selects this namespace, and with no allow rule for payments, it drops the connection.
Meanwhile your same-namespace smoke test passes green — which misleads you into thinking the app and service are healthy.
The fix is a targeted ingress allow rule keyed to the payments pod label: permit role=payments.
Now on a match the policy forwards to the api service, which reaches the app — payments connects.
The lesson: once a policy selects pods, every allow must be named on purpose — the boundary is the incident, not the code.

networkpolicy-boundaries.title: The gold artifact: a deny-by-default policy plus one scoped allow
networkpolicy-boundaries.subtitle: network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md ships this manifest. It closes the namespace, then re-opens exactly one ingress — payments pods on 8080 — and nothing else. Label-scoped, not CIDR-guessed.
networkpolicy-boundaries.code:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-default-deny-plus-payments
  namespace: api
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: api
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              role: payments
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 8080
# Verify (the proof, not the apply):
#   kubectl describe networkpolicy api-default-deny-plus-payments -n api
#   kubectl exec -n payments deploy/checkout -- curl -v --max-time 5 http://api.api.svc:8080/health   # MUST pass
#   kubectl exec -n default   deploy/scratch  -- curl -v --max-time 5 http://api.api.svc:8080/health   # MUST time out

steps.label: The boundary target
steps.note: podSelector app=api scopes the policy to your service's pods. This is the surface you are drawing a boundary around — get it wrong and you protect the wrong pods.

steps.label: Ingress-only = deny-by-default inbound
steps.note: Listing Ingress in policyTypes flips the default: any inbound not matched below is now DENIED. This single line is what caused the payments outage — and what you're now stating on purpose.

steps.label: The one allow, keyed to a label
steps.note: Allow ingress FROM pods labeled role=payments. Label-scoped, not an IP or CIDR — pods get new IPs on every reschedule, so a CIDR allow rots. This is the rejected-option boundary made concrete.

steps.label: Scope the port too
steps.note: Allow only TCP 8080. An allow with no ports opens every port on the pod — a quiet over-grant a reviewer will catch.

steps.label: Proof #1 — the allowed path passes
steps.note: curl from a payments pod MUST return 200. If it hangs, your podSelector label doesn't match the real pod labels — the classic silent miss.

steps.label: Proof #2 — the denied path times out
steps.note: curl from an unlisted namespace MUST time out, not refuse. A timeout (dropped SYN) is the signature of a working deny; a fast connection-refused means the policy isn't selecting the pod at all.

networkpolicy-boundaries.caption: The boundary is proven when line 21 passes AND line 22 times out. One without the other is half a proof: open-to-everyone, or closed-to-everyone.

networkpolicy-boundaries.text: The senior tell in Kubernetes networking: a deny is a timeout, a missing service is a refuse. A dropped SYN from a NetworkPolicy makes the client hang until timeout; a wrong port or absent endpoint returns connection-refused immediately. If your 'blocked' pod gets refused fast, the policy isn't even selecting the target — you're debugging the wrong layer. Read the failure mode before you write the allow.

networkpolicy-boundaries.question: A reviewer challenges your NetworkPolicy: 'You proved payments can reach the service. Show me it's actually a boundary and not just open.' What is the exact evidence that answers them?
options: The output of `kubectl apply` showing the policy was created successfully.
A `curl -v` from a payments pod returning 200, plus a `curl -v` from an unlisted namespace pod timing out — both captured against the same service.
A screenshot of the YAML manifest with the ingress rule highlighted.
A `dig` showing the service name resolves to a ClusterIP.
networkpolicy-boundaries.explanation: A boundary is two claims — allowed traffic passes AND denied traffic is dropped — so it takes two observations. Only option 2 shows both: the allowed path returning 200 and the denied path timing out. `apply` (1) proves the YAML parsed, the manifest (3) proves intent not effect, and `dig` (4) proves DNS, which was never the cause. The deny half is the part the outage made everyone forget to test.

networkpolicy-boundaries.intro: Prove your boundary holds — no vibes, three layers of proof:
items: Decision proof: your packet names the constraint (deny-by-default on ns=api) BEFORE the policy, and states the rejected option (a CIDR-based allow) with why it rots — pod IPs change on reschedule.

Operational proof — allow side: `kubectl exec` a curl from a pod that SHOULD reach the service returns 200. If it hangs, your podSelector label doesn't match the real pod labels; run `kubectl get pod --show-labels` and reconcile.
Operational proof — deny side: `kubectl exec` a curl from a pod that should NOT reach it TIMES OUT (not refuses). A fast refuse means the policy isn't selecting your target pods at all.

Read the boundary back from the cluster: `kubectl describe networkpolicy` shows exactly one allowed source and one allowed port — no empty `from` (which allows all) and no empty `ports` (which opens every port).

Transfer proof: name what changes in a stricter environment (a regulated cluster adds egress deny + DNS-only allow, so CoreDNS itself needs an explicit egress rule or every pod loses name resolution).

prompts: Explain why empty app logs plus a client-side timeout points at a NetworkPolicy deny and not an application bug — trace where the SYN dies.
Your reviewer asks why you keyed the allow to a pod label instead of the payments pods' IP range. Answer using your own packet.
Walk the difference between a connection that TIMES OUT and one that is REFUSED, and what each tells you about whether the policy is selecting the right pods.

packet-capture-plan.outcome: Take a real intermittent-reachability failure — a service that works for some clients but fails for others after a DNS, TLS, routing, or policy change — and write a Packet Capture Plan: WHERE you will tap, the exact BPF filter, the single hypothesis each capture kills, and the boundary you will not cross. Then commit it to network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md.
packet-capture-plan.proof: The 'Capture Plan' section of network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md: at least two capture points on the path (client-side, LB, pod/host), a scoped BPF filter for each (host/port, not 'capture everything'), the hypothesis each tap disqualifies, and an explicit stop rule. A reviewer agrees your FIRST capture is the one most likely to prove where the path breaks — DNS, TLS, route, or policy — for the least data.
packet-capture-plan.unlock: Your plan names the capture points, a scoped filter per point, the hypothesis each kills, and a boundary you will not tap — before you run a single tcpdump.
packet-capture-plan.doNotClaim: Do not claim you have a capture plan if it is just 'run tcpdump on the box'. An unscoped, single-point capture on one machine is a hope, not a plan. A plan taps BOTH sides of the suspect edge so the packet either arrives or it does not — that is the whole point.

packet-capture-plan.text: It is hour three of a P1: checkout works from the office VPN and fails from half the mobile users, and someone already 'fixed' the app code twice. A staff SRE ignores the code, opens two terminals, and runs one tcpdump at the load balancer and one inside the pod — and in ninety seconds proves the SYN never reaches the pod. The bug was a NetworkPolicy, not a line of code.

Intermittent reachability after a DNS, TLS, routing, or policy change is the classic trap: the symptom looks like application code, but the cause lives in name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or a firewall rule. A capture plan decides WHERE to put the tap so the packets tell you which layer actually broke — this is Section 1 of the incident packet you carry through this module.

packet-capture-plan.prompt: A service fails for ~40% of clients after a rollout. Your first instinct is to run `tcpdump -i any` on the affected pod and read the trace. Before you do — what is wrong with starting there? Answer before reading on.
packet-capture-plan.reveal: A single capture on ONE end can only tell you what arrived, never what was sent. If the pod sees no SYN, you cannot tell 'the client never sent it' from 'a route/NAT/NetworkPolicy dropped it in flight' — the two failures look identical from one tap. The senior move is to capture on BOTH sides of the suspect edge at once: `tcpdump host <client> and port 443` at the LB AND in the pod. The packet either crosses the edge or it does not — and now the drop point is proven, not guessed.

packet-capture-plan.intro: Writing the Capture Plan, one line at a time. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
packet-capture-plan.code:
## 1. Capture Plan  (service: checkout.svc, symptom: works for VPN, fails for ~40% mobile after policy change)
# Confirm resolution first — is DNS even returning the right VIP for failing clients?
dig +short checkout.example.com            # kill-test: split-horizon / stale record
# TAP #1 — load balancer: does the client SYN + TLS ClientHello arrive at all?
tcpdump -ni eth0 'host 203.0.113.10 and tcp port 443' -c 200 -w lb.pcap
# TAP #2 — inside the pod: does that same SYN cross the NetworkPolicy?
kubectl debug -it checkout-pod --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- \
  tcpdump -ni eth0 'tcp port 8443 and tcp[tcpflags] & tcp-syn != 0' -c 50 -w pod.pcap
# Boundary: do NOT tap the billing path or capture unfiltered 'any' (PII + noise).
# Stop rule: SYN in lb.pcap but absent in pod.pcap -> NetworkPolicy drop, decide. Or 15 min.
steps: Frame the capture: Name the service, the symptom, and the recent change (policy) in the header. A capture with no hypothesis is a data dump.
Rule out DNS first — cheapest layer: dig is a two-second kill-test. Split-horizon DNS or a stale record explains 'some clients fail' before any packet capture. If the VIP is wrong, stop here.
TAP #1 at the LB — scoped to host + port: 'host <client> and tcp port 443' — NOT 'tcpdump -i any'. The filter proves the ClientHello arrives at the edge, and keeps the pcap small and PII-bounded.

TAP #2 in the pod — the SAME flow, the other side: kubectl debug + netshoot taps inside the pod netns. The tcp-syn filter isolates connection setup. If the SYN is in lb.pcap but not here, the NetworkPolicy dropped it — silently, exactly as they do.
The boundary: Never capture unfiltered on a shared node: it sweeps up other tenants' traffic (PII, secrets in flight). Scope every tap, and name what you will NOT tap.
The stop rule: SYN present upstream + absent downstream = proven drop point. A concrete threshold turns 'keep capturing' into 'decide'.
packet-capture-plan.commonMistake: Proves nothing — a data dump with a hunch

packet-capture-plan.title: A capture plan taps both sides of the suspect edge, scoped and hypothesis-first
packet-capture-plan.text: Pick the edge the diagnosis suspects, tap on BOTH sides simultaneously, scope each tap with a tight BPF filter (host + port), and name the hypothesis each capture kills. The invariant: a captured packet is evidence a drop is not — it proves which layer broke.

packet-capture-plan.title: Where to tap on the request path
packet-capture-plan.subtitle: One request crosses five trust boundaries: DNS, TLS handshake, LB, NetworkPolicy, pod. Each has a layer that can silently break it. The capture plan taps BEFORE and AFTER the suspect edge (LB → NetworkPolicy → pod) so a dropped SYN is caught where it dies. Auth and billing are deliberately out of scope.

nodes.label: Service Pod
nodes.description: TAP #2 — does SYN cross the policy?

legend.label: capture points (both sides of the edge)
layers that fail silently: DNS, TLS, policy
kept out of scope on purpose

storyboard.say: The request starts at the client, which first asks the resolver for an address before it can reach anything.
With a name resolved, the client sends a TLS SYN to port 443, opening the real request path we care about.
The load balancer forwards that connection inward, the first hop where a dropped SYN can vanish without a trace.
The NetworkPolicy is the silent gate: it either allows the packet through or drops it, and drops leave no log.
So we tap on both sides of the suspect edge at once: one tcpdump at the load balancer, one inside the pod.
The pod's downstream billing path is deliberately out of scope, so we don't chase auth or payment red herrings.
If the SYN shows at the balancer but never in the pod, the policy killed it. A captured packet is evidence a drop can't give you.

packet-capture-plan.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You captured on the pod and saw no SYN — so the client is broken, right?' Why is that conclusion unproven, and what capture plan proves it?
options: It is proven — no SYN at the pod means the client never sent one; close the ticket on the client team.

A single downstream capture cannot distinguish 'never sent' from 'dropped in flight'. Capture the SAME flow on both sides — LB and pod — so a SYN present at the LB but absent in the pod localizes the drop to the NetworkPolicy or route between them.
Re-run `tcpdump -i any` for longer on the pod until a SYN eventually shows up.
Skip captures and add more application logging, since the pod is clearly the problem.
packet-capture-plan.explanation: One tap only tells you what arrived at that tap — absence at the pod is consistent with BOTH a client that never sent and an in-flight drop (NetworkPolicy, NAT, asymmetric route). The plan that proves it captures the same flow on both sides of the suspect edge: SYN present upstream + absent downstream isolates the drop to that segment. Options 1 and 4 assume the answer; option 3 just adds noise.

firewall-denial-repair.text: The service is green on the dashboard, healthy from the office VPN, and dead from the new region — and three engineers are already rewriting the retry logic. The denial isn't in the code they're editing; it's a firewall rule that never let the packet arrive.

A production service reachable from some clients but denied for others is almost never an application bug — it's name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or network policy. This lesson turns that intermittent denial into a traced, evidenced repair packet you carry into the capstone.

firewall-denial-repair.prompt: curl to the service hangs and eventually times out from Region B, but works instantly from Region A. Your teammate says 'the app is slow, add a timeout retry.' Before you agree — what's wrong with that read?
firewall-denial-repair.reveal: A hang-then-timeout is the signature of a silent DROP, not a slow app. A busy app REJECTS fast (connection refused / 500 in milliseconds) or answers late — it does not black-hole. When the TCP handshake never completes (SYN sent, no SYN-ACK) for one CIDR but not another, a firewall or NetworkPolicy is dropping the packet before your code ever runs. Adding retries just makes the denial slower to surface.

firewall-denial-repair.intro: Proving the denial — dig, curl, openssl, then the NetworkPolicy. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
firewall-denial-repair.code:
# 1. DNS resolves fine from Region B — rule out name resolution
dig +short service.example.com
# 203.0.113.10   → same IP as Region A. DNS is NOT the denial.

# 2. curl hangs, then times out — the drop signature (no fast reject)
curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://service.example.com/health
# * Trying 203.0.113.10:443...
# * Connection timed out after 5001 ms   ← SYN sent, no SYN-ACK = silent DROP

# 3. Confirm it dies BEFORE TLS — openssl can't even open the socket
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com
# connect: Connection timed out   ← never reached the TLS layer

# 4. Find the policy that selects the pod and omits Region B's CIDR
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-ingress -n prod
# Spec:
#   PodSelector: app=orders
#   Ingress:
#     From: ipBlock 10.10.0.0/16 (Region A)   ← Region B 10.40.0.0/16 MISSING
#   default: DROP everything not explicitly allowed
steps: Rule out DNS first: dig returns the same IP from both regions — name resolution is not the denial. Eliminating the cheapest suspect first keeps the trace honest.

curl reveals the drop signature: '-v' with a short --connect-timeout: a HANG then timeout means SYN sent, no SYN-ACK. That black-hole is a firewall DROP, not a slow app. A busy app would refuse or answer, not vanish.
openssl confirms it dies before TLS: The socket never opens, so this is not a certificate or SNI problem. The denial is below TLS — at the routing/policy layer.

Name the offending rule: The NetworkPolicy selects app=orders and allows only Region A's ipBlock; the default-deny drops Region B's 10.40.0.0/16. This is the suspect edge, now proven — the repair is to add the missing CIDR, scoped to the needed ports.

storyboard.say: The service is green on the dashboard, but dead from Region B. Follow the actual packet, not the retry code three engineers are rewriting.
First hop: the Region B client resolves the name. If DNS returns nothing, the failure is here, before any connection begins.
DNS resolved, so the client connects to the IP. Route and NAT translation is the next place a packet can silently go astray.
The route sends a SYN to the firewall and NetworkPolicy. This is the decision hop where the denial actually lives.
Region A's CIDR is allowlisted, so the firewall accepts and forwards it onward to the TLS handshake.
Region B's CIDR is not allowed, so the firewall issues a silent DROP. No SYN-ACK, no app log, no error the code could catch.
Only survivors reach TLS and then the pod. The app never saw Region B, so proving the drop with command output points repair at the rule, not the code.

The scenario data and safe helper functions are provided. Complete the one decision function,

    (30, 'ALLOW', 443, '172.20.0.0/16'),

    ('legacy-host',  '172.16.99.9', 443),

]

def to_int(ip):
    a, b, c, d = (int(x) for x in ip.split('.'))
    return (a << 24) | (b << 16) | (c << 8) | d

def cidr_bounds(cidr):
    net, prefix = cidr.split('/')

    ilo, ihi = cidr_bounds(inner)

firewall-denial-repair.question: A reviewer challenges your packet: 'How do I know this was a firewall denial and not the application failing?' Which single piece of evidence answers that?
options: The application log shows a 500 error and a stack trace for the failed request.

curl -v hangs and times out at the TCP connect stage (SYN, no SYN-ACK) from the denied CIDR while succeeding from the allowed one, and kubectl describe networkpolicy shows that CIDR is not in the ingress allowlist.
The dashboard shows elevated latency for the affected region.
Restarting the pod temporarily made the errors go away.
firewall-denial-repair.explanation: Only option 2 proves a policy-layer denial: the connection dies before TLS (so the app never ran), it fails only for the denied CIDR, and the offending rule is named. An app 500 (1) means the packet DID arrive — the opposite conclusion. Latency (3) and a pod restart (4) are symptoms that don't distinguish a drop from an app fault.

items: Your packet traces the path in order (DNS → route → TLS → policy) and eliminates each cheap suspect with an inspection-hook output, not a hunch.
The denial is shown as a connection that never completes (curl hang/timeout or openssl connect failure) from the denied source — while the same command succeeds from an allowed source.
The offending rule is named: the exact firewall entry or NetworkPolicy ipBlock, and the specific CIDR/port that was missing.
The repair is least-privilege: it adds only the CIDR and ports the trace proved were denied. You can state which broader option (e.g. 0.0.0.0/0) you rejected and why.
Post-repair re-verification is attached: the same curl from the previously denied client now returns 200, and the allowed client still works (no regression).

zero-trust-access.doNotClaim: Do not claim 'zero-trust access is enforced' because a request succeeded from your laptop. A pass from one client on one network proves that path, not the policy. Until you show a deny that SHOULD deny and an allow that SHOULD allow — each with hook output — you have a demo, not a verified access boundary.

zero-trust-access.text: The service is green on your machine and paging in production: half the clients get 200s, the other half hang, and three engineers are already deep in the application code — where the bug is not. The real break is one layer down: a name that resolves differently, a cert nobody trusts, a route that only goes one way, or a NetworkPolicy that quietly denies the pod.

Zero-trust means every hop re-verifies identity and authorization instead of trusting the network — so a failure is never 'the network is down', it is a specific hop refusing a specific caller. This lesson closes Network Debugging & Security: it turns 'it works for me' into an inspectable decision packet that survives a reviewer replaying your evidence.

zero-trust-access.prompt: A production service works from the office network but fails from the new cluster. Before touching code, what is the single fastest first move — and why would testing the application logic be a trap?
zero-trust-access.reveal: Trace the path, do not read the code. Zero-trust adds re-verification at every hop, so 'works here, fails there' is almost always a hop-specific trust decision: the new cluster resolves the name to a different IP, presents a client cert the server does not trust, takes a route the return path never mirrors, or lives in a namespace a NetworkPolicy denies. `dig` + `curl -v` + `kubectl describe networkpolicy` from the FAILING client localizes the break in minutes; re-reading application code confirms only that the code you own is innocent — which you already suspected.

zero-trust-access.intro: The verification trail inside network_path_debug_and_incident_packet.md. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
zero-trust-access.code:
# Verification trail — run from the FAILING client, not your laptop

# Hop 1 — Name resolution: does the name point where I think?
$ dig +short api.internal.svc
10.4.7.22        # office resolver -> old IP; cluster resolver -> 10.8.3.9 (DRIFT)

# Hop 2 — Route / TLS reachability: can I even open the socket + who answers?
$ curl -v --connect-timeout 5 https://api.internal.svc/health
*   Trying 10.8.3.9:443...
* SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate  # cert not trusted

# Hop 3 — Certificate trust: whose CA signed this, and is it expired?
$ openssl s_client -connect 10.8.3.9:443 -servername api.internal.svc </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -dates
issuer=CN=mesh-ca-2023          # rotated CA; failing clients still trust mesh-ca-2022
notAfter=Jun 30 00:00:00 2026 GMT

# Hop 4 — Authorization: does policy actually admit this caller's namespace/labels?
$ kubectl describe networkpolicy api-allow -n prod
Ingress: From: podSelector app=gateway   # allows gateway pods ONLY
# failing client is app=batch-runner -> no matching allow rule -> DENY

# Finding: two independent breaks -> resolver drift (Hop 1) AND policy deny (Hop 4)
steps: Hop 1 — resolve from the failing client: dig +short from the failing network, not yours. Same name, two answers = resolver/split-horizon drift. This alone explains 'works for some clients'.
Hop 2 — one curl -v spans route + TLS: 'Trying <IP>' confirms the route opened; the SSL line localizes the break to certificate trust, not the app. curl -v is the cheapest disqualifier on the path.
Hop 3 — name the CA, don't guess: openssl prints issuer + dates. A rotated CA (2022 -> 2023) that failing clients never got is the classic zero-trust break: identity, not connectivity.

Hop 4 — read the policy, don't assume: kubectl describe networkpolicy shows the ACTUAL allow rule. app=gateway only means app=batch-runner is denied by default-deny — a policy decision, invisible to the application.
The finding is a layer, backed by output: Two independent breaks. The packet records BOTH with evidence; a reviewer replays each hook and confirms. This is operational proof, not description.

storyboard.say: The call starts at the client. Before it reaches the pod, it must survive four separate checkpoints — no hop trusts the last.
Checkpoint one: DNS. The client asks for a name and gets an IP. Half your clients fail here on a stale or wrong answer.
If the name is dead — NXDOMAIN or a stale IP pointing nowhere — trust is denied at DNS, long before any code runs.
A good name connects to the IP, then the route or NAT forwards you to the host on port 443, ready to prove identity.
Checkpoint two: mTLS. You present a cert. Untrusted or expired, and the handshake refuses you — this is the other half hanging.
Checkpoint three: NetworkPolicy. Even a proven caller is checked for authorization — no matching allow rule means denied.
Only a caller that clears name, cert, route, and policy reaches the pod. ALLOW is earned at every hop, never assumed.
So the bug is never 'the network is down' — it's one named hop refusing one caller. Localize the hop, read its evidence, then fix.

zero-trust-access.text: The zero-trust tell that separates operators from guessers: default-deny is not a bug, it is the design. When a caller fails, the senior move is 'which allow rule was it missing, and should it exist?' — not 'the network is blocking us'. A NetworkPolicy denying an unlisted caller is the system working; the question is whether that caller earned an allow, proven by identity, not by IP range.

zero-trust-access.question: A reviewer challenges: 'You say zero-trust access works — prove it, don't describe it.' Which single piece of evidence actually proves it?
options: A screenshot of the service returning 200 from your laptop on the office VPN.
The NetworkPolicy YAML committed to the repo, showing an allow rule exists.
Paired hook output: a caller that SHOULD be denied getting denied (kubectl/openssl), AND the intended caller getting allowed — each replayable from the failing/passing client.
A statement that mTLS is enabled mesh-wide and all pods have sidecars.
zero-trust-access.explanation: Zero-trust is an authorization boundary, so proof is a boundary test: the deny that should deny AND the allow that should allow, each with replayable evidence (openssl for identity, kubectl describe networkpolicy for authorization). A 200 from one trusted client (1) proves one happy path. Committed YAML (2) proves intent, not enforcement. 'mTLS is on' (4) is a description. Only paired, replayable allow/deny output is inspectable proof.

network-incident-runbook.text: The service is green on your laptop and 500ing for half the fleet — and the room is already three commits deep into the app code. The outage is not in the app. It is on an arrow between two boxes, and nobody has traced the arrow.

You mapped systems and read routes in earlier lessons; the incident runbook is where that reasoning meets a live partial outage. The failure that ends careers here is debugging application code while the real fault is name resolution, certificate trust, route asymmetry, or a network policy.

network-incident-runbook.prompt: A production endpoint works for some clients and fails for others right after a deploy. Where do you look first — the application logs, or somewhere earlier on the path?
network-incident-runbook.reveal: Earlier. 'Some clients, not others' is the signature of a network cause, not an app bug — app bugs usually fail for everyone or no one. Split traffic points at DNS returning different records, a route that is asymmetric, a TLS SAN mismatch on one host, or a NetworkPolicy that only some pods hit. Trace the path before you touch the code.

network-incident-runbook.intro: Four hooks that isolate the layer. Follow one complete evidence path before attempting the simulation lab.
network-incident-runbook.code:
# Layer 1 — DNS: what IP does THIS client resolve to?
dig +short service.example.com
# → 10.0.4.7   (a healthy client resolves 10.0.5.9 — split answer!)

# Layer 2 — Route + policy: can we even reach the host?
kubectl describe networkpolicy allow-orders | grep -A2 Ingress
# → from: podSelector app=web   (curl client isn't 'web' → denied)

# Layer 3 — TLS: is the cert trusted and does the SAN match?
openssl s_client -connect service.example.com:443 -servername service.example.com </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'subject=|Verify'
# → subject=CN=old.example.com   Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify)

# Layer 4 — HTTP: only now, ask the app
curl -v https://service.example.com/health
# → * SSL certificate problem  (fails BEFORE any app code runs)
steps: DNS first: dig +short shows the record THIS client gets. A split answer (different IPs per client) explains 'some clients fail' without touching the app.
Route + policy: kubectl describe networkpolicy reveals a podSelector that admits 'web' but not your test pod — asymmetric reachability, not an app fault.
TLS trust: openssl s_client exposes the cert subject and verify code. Return code 21 with a stale CN is a SAN mismatch — the handshake fails before HTTP exists.
HTTP last: curl -v fails at 'SSL certificate problem' — proof the fault is TLS, not the service. The app never ran. Case closed on the correct layer.

network-incident-runbook.title: The request path — and where it can lie
network-incident-runbook.subtitle: One request from client to service, layer by layer. Each hop is a place the outage can hide: DNS resolution, IP routing, TLS trust, then HTTP. The decision fork asks 'did this layer answer honestly?' — the suspect edge (TLS trust on one host) is marked, and the blast radius is a subset of clients getting a cert error.
network-incident-runbook.caption: Diagnose layer by layer. The first hop that lies is the cause; everything downstream is a symptom.

storyboard.say: The service is green on your laptop but 500ing for half the fleet. Don't touch app code yet — trace one request down the layers.
Layer one: the client must turn a hostname into an address. DNS resolves the host before anything else can happen.
With an IP in hand, routing and network policy decide whether packets actually reach the host. Route asymmetry hides here.
The request reaches the host and TLS begins. This is the decision fork: did the certificate answer honestly, or is trust broken?
If the cert is trusted, TLS passes and HTTP finally answers the service. That's the honest, healthy path.
But on one host the SAN doesn't match, so TLS fails. Only clients hitting that host get a cert error — the blast radius.
That's why half return 200 and half 5xx. Name the lying layer — TLS trust — its blast radius and evidence before proposing any fix.

network-incident-runbook.text: The senior tell is the invalidation line. 'Some clients, not others' plus a stated invalidation condition — 'if openssl verifies cleanly on a failing client, my TLS theory is dead' — is what separates a proven runbook from a plausible story. Distinguish stale from lost, and reachable-for-some from down: those words set the incident's urgency.

network-incident-runbook.question: A reviewer challenges your incident packet: 'You proved the fix worked — but did you prove the network was the cause and not the app?' What single piece of evidence answers this best?
options: The service returned 200 after you redeployed the application.
openssl s_client output showing Verify return code 21 and a stale SAN captured BEFORE any app change, from a failing client.
A screenshot of the dashboard turning green.
The app logs had no errors during the incident.
network-incident-runbook.explanation: The openssl output isolates the layer: it shows the TLS handshake failing on a failing client before HTTP or app code is reached, so the cause is certificate trust, not the application. A 200 after redeploy (0) and a green dashboard (2) prove the fix ran but not what the cause was — they are unfalsifiable. Quiet app logs (3) are consistent with the app never being the problem, but do not localize the fault the way layer-specific evidence does.
